name: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, primary
lead: What to do with the pancreatic primary once differentiation and the exact Ki-67 are known — observe it, enucleate it, or do a formal oncologic resection — and where this page stops and the NELM pathway begins.
gatelabel: The decision in front of you

gates.name: 1 · Differentiation and grade
crit: Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour, not a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma
An exact Ki-67 proliferative index reported as a number, not a range, with the mitotic count per 2 mm²
Two of synaptophysin, chromogranin A and INSM1 positive, with a broad-spectrum keratin
Acinar cell carcinoma and the other neuroendocrine-marker mimics excluded where the morphology is unusual
Functional status recorded as a clinical and biochemical judgement, not an immunohistochemical one
gates.ask: Is this a well-differentiated tumour, and do I have a number for Ki-67 rather than a range?

standard.t: Grade with the WHO 2019 criteria and insist on the exact Ki-67 index and the mitotic rate per 2 mm², with the raw counts reported.
standard.pref: Every specimen, primary or metastatic, biopsy or resection, with at least 500 assessable tumour cells and no crush artefact. Ki-67 is counted in the hot spot of highest nuclear labelling; the mitotic rate is counted in the areas of highest density, per 2 mm², which equals 10 high-power fields at 40× with a 0.5 mm ocular field.
standard.avoid: Do not accept a report that says "neuroendocrine tumour" or "neuroendocrine carcinoma" without a grade and without the parameters used to assign it. NCCN states plainly that such a report is inadequate for prognostication and therapy and inappropriate for pathology reporting.
standard.note: Where mitotic rate and Ki-67 give different grades, the higher grade is assigned. Where several blocks are available, stain the block with the highest mitotic index and grade on the highest index; with synchronous specimens from several sites, stain at least one block from each.

standard.t: Separate a well-differentiated grade 3 tumour from a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma before any treatment decision — they are different diseases that share a Ki-67 range.
standard.pref: Any pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasm with Ki-67 above 20%. In 31 well-differentiated tumours with a morphologically apparent high-grade component, 21 of them pancreatic, median disease-specific survival was 55 months (range 16-119), with 2-year and 5-year survival of 88-89% and 48-49%. The institutional comparators were 162 months for low and intermediate grade pancreatic well-differentiated tumours (2-year and 5-year 97% and 90%) and 16 months for pancreatic poorly differentiated carcinoma (24% and 24%), p<0.001. Genotype separates them: a DAXX, ATRX or MEN1 mutation was present in 35 of 63 (57%) low and intermediate grade tumours and in 3 of 4 sequenced transformed tumours against 0 of 28 carcinomas; Rb protein was lost in 0% of well-differentiated tumours of any grade against 59% of carcinomas; and p53 immunoreactivity was abnormal in 0% against 56%.
standard.avoid: Do not route a well-differentiated G3 tumour down a small-cell carcinoma pathway, and do not treat a poorly differentiated carcinoma as a NET because the Ki-67 happens to be 25%. NANETS reports a multi-institutional pathological review in which only 44 of 107 resected pancreatic tumours originally called poorly differentiated carcinoma actually were; that review is not in this page's full-text depot and the figure is quoted as NANETS states it.
standard.note: Read the survival contrast carefully. In the stage-matched analysis restricted to stage IV, pancreatic grade 1-2 well-differentiated tumours and those with a high-grade component showed no statistically significant difference in disease-specific survival, and both did far better than poorly differentiated carcinoma (median 61 against 16 months, p<0.001; hazard ratios 0.17 and 0.16 against carcinoma as reference). The 55-against-162-month comparison is unmatched, and it is the one the abstract leads with. The 31 cases were assembled by searching two pathology archives for grade discrepancy, so the series cannot say how often this happens, the genotype contrast rests on four prospectively sequenced tumours against literature controls, and 6 of the 31 were biopsies only in which the coexisting lower-grade component was inferred from clinical history rather than seen. In challenging cases, particularly in the pancreas, NCCN lists Rb, p53, p16, ATRX and DAXX as an optional panel to help distinguish G3 NET from carcinoma, read together with the clinical, functional-imaging and molecular picture. See gate 8 for what each diagnosis then means.

standard.t: Treat a grade obtained from a needle biopsy as a floor, not a fact — biopsy systematically understates grade in G2 disease.
standard.pref: Any observation-versus-resection decision that rests on grade. In 46 tumours sampled by EUS-FNA at one centre, 33 of which were resected and available for comparison, agreement between readers was excellent within each modality (Pearson r-squared 0.93 on cytology and 0.94 on the resection specimen, both p<0.001, with no grade disagreement between readers) - but agreement between cytological and histological grade was poor: kappa 0.21 (p=0.09), rising only to 0.24 (p=0.06) when restricted to the 27 cases with at least 200 cells counted, and no better at a 5% cut-off than at 2%. Cytology under-graded systematically: 10 of 14 histological G2 tumours (71%) were called cytological G1, and histological Ki-67 averaged 1.3 times the cytological value. Cytological grade still separated the worst group - actuarial progression-free survival 10 plus or minus 4 months for cytological G3 against 29 plus or minus 7 for G2 and 68 plus or minus 10 for G1 (p<0.0001) - but cytological G1 and G2 did not differ for progression-free or overall survival.
standard.avoid: Do not promise a patient that a G1 biopsy means a G1 tumour. NANETS reports agreement of tumour grade between EUS-FNA cytology and the resection specimen in under 50% of G2 and G3 cases, and areas with Ki-67 of 2% or less were common even within G2 tumours. The only prospective study of fine-needle core biopsy in non-functional tumours found 83% concordance, in 30 patients; that study is quoted from the NANETS text and is not in this page's full-text depot.
standard.note: Two cautions on the study itself. The four cytological G3 patients who drive the significant survival separation were all locally advanced, node-positive or metastatic at diagnosis, so cytological G3 may be marking stage rather than grade; and the concordance analysis could only include the resected tumours, so nothing in it describes how cytology performs in the small lesions actually being watched. Progression-free survival was also calculated independently of whether the tumour was removed, mixing resected and unresected patients in the same curves. Where additional tissue is needed for immunohistochemistry, add core biopsy to aspiration where it is available. [EXPERTISE]

alt.t: Biopsy is not obligatory to decide to observe a small incidental lesion with the imaging phenotype of a neuroendocrine tumour.
alt.pref: An asymptomatic sub-centimetre lesion with characteristic arterial enhancement where the plan is surveillance whatever the grade. NANETS states that in such patients biopsy is not routinely necessary to confirm the diagnosis before deciding to observe.
alt.avoid: Do not skip tissue when the diagnosis is genuinely in question, when grade would change the plan, or when the lesion is 1-2 cm and the observe-or-resect decision is live - that is exactly the decision grade is meant to inform. And know that the guidelines disagree here. ENETS 2023, read in full, states that a suspected nonfunctioning tumour under 2 cm with positive somatostatin-receptor imaging should be confirmed histologically or cytologically where possible (level 3 evidence, grade B), and notes DAXX and ATRX loss and alternative lengthening of telomeres as independent adverse prognostic factors particularly in tumours of 2 cm or less. The 2025 MEN1 recommendations go the other way again and find no role for routine EUS-guided biopsy in that syndrome. See the honest section and approval 11.
alt.note: The ASPEN study required a positive fine-needle aspirate or biopsy, or a positive 68Ga-labelled DOTA PET, before enrolment - but in practice 170 of its 500 patients (34%) never had an aspirate, it was negative in a further 45 (9%), and grade was not evaluable in 68 of the 285 who did have one (23.9%). So its reassuring surveillance figures come from a population in which the diagnosis was often established by receptor PET alone and in which the surveillance arm has no histological characterisation at all.

alt.t: Order molecular profiling where the disease is locoregionally unresectable or metastatic and the patient is a candidate for systemic therapy.
alt.pref: Tumour tissue is preferred; circulating tumour DNA is an option when tissue testing is not feasible. ENETS encourages molecular profiling in neuroendocrine carcinoma specifically, to identify new targets, while saying plainly that the targets are not yet established.
alt.avoid: Do not profile a small localised G1 tumour that is going to be observed or enucleated: nothing in the result changes that decision, and there is no established targeted therapy in this setting.

avoid.t: Do not let a hormone immunostain decide whether the tumour is functional.
avoid.pref: Functional status is a clinical syndrome plus biochemical evidence of inappropriately raised hormone — that is the ENETS definition and it is what gate 3 works from.
avoid.avoid: NCCN states that hormone staining by immunohistochemistry is not helpful and that a positive stain does not mean there is a functional tumour. Chasing a positive insulin stain in an asymptomatic normoglycaemic patient produces an operation nobody needed.

avoid.t: Do not accept the diagnostic label "carcinoma with neuroendocrine features".
avoid.pref: Ask for a definite WHO classification. Where the histology is genuinely ambiguous the report should say so, recommend clinical correlation and recommend a broad next-generation sequencing panel.
avoid.avoid: Adenocarcinomas of the GI tract often express neuroendocrine markers patchily with no survival or management significance, and that patchy expression is a common route into the wrong pathway. In higher-grade pancreatic neoplasms, trypsin, chymotrypsin and BCL10 help exclude an acinar cell carcinoma expressing neuroendocrine markers.

gates.name: 2 · Stage the primary, and read the two PETs
crit: Multiphasic CT or MRI of the abdomen, with arterial and portal venous phases, covering the whole pancreas
Somatostatin-receptor PET/CT or PET/MRI where receptor status or occult metastatic disease would change the plan
Chest CT, and FDG-PET where the tumour is G2 or higher
Main pancreatic duct calibre, tumour calcification and cystic morphology recorded explicitly
Liver and nodal status stated before any operation is booked
gates.ask: Is this disease confined to the pancreas, and does a discordant pair of PET scans tell me the grade on the biopsy is wrong?

standard.t: If staging shows hepatic metastases, the hepatic disease is the NELM pathway from here — this page covers the primary only.
standard.pref: Hand off at this gate, by name, as soon as liver deposits are seen. The NELM page carries hepatic tumour burden and distribution, cytoreduction thresholds, liver-directed modality choice, systemic sequencing for grade 1–2 and high-grade disease, carcinoid-crisis precautions and the transplant question. It also carries the decision about resecting the pancreatic primary when liver metastases are present, where NANETS reached no consensus and the majority view was that resection may help only in selected circumstances.
standard.avoid: Do not make the primary-resection decision in metastatic disease on this page. Two specific warnings travel with the patient: NCCN states that pancreatoduodenectomy in metastatic disease is usually not curative and affects liver-directed therapy long term, and that liver-directed therapies for hepatic metastases after pancreatoduodenectomy carry an increased risk of cholangitis and liver abscess. That makes the sequence a joint decision between this gate and the NELM pathway, not a pancreatic one.
standard.note: Locoregionally advanced unresectable disease without liver metastases is also outside this page's scope: it is a systemic-therapy decision and NCCN's pancreatic NET systemic principles apply.

standard.t: Use somatostatin-receptor PET rather than octreotide scintigraphy, and read it together with multiphase contrast CT or MRI in the same sitting where the scanner allows it.
standard.pref: Staging where occult metastatic disease would change the operation, and localising a primary in a patient who presents with metastases. In a prospective single-centre study of 131 patients imaged with all three modalities and read independently and blind, 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT detected 847 of 891 lesions, 95.1% (95% CI 92.4-96.8), against 404 of 891, 45.3% (37.9-52.9), for anatomic imaging and 275 of 891, 30.9% (25.0-37.5), for 111In-pentetreotide SPECT/CT (p<0.001 for both comparisons), and the PET changed the management recommendation in 43 of 131 patients (32.8%). A previously unknown primary was found in 4 of 14 patients (28.6%).
standard.avoid: Do not read the PET alone. Contrast CT or MRI is what identifies the receptor-negative deposits, and NCCN requires the two together. Acceptable tracers are 68Ga-DOTATATE, 68Ga-DOTATOC and 64Cu-DOTATATE; a lesion counts as receptor-positive when uptake exceeds liver, and the modified Krenning score runs 0 none, 1 very low, 2 at or below liver, 3 above liver, 4 above spleen.
standard.note: Grade C, downgraded on the full-text read, and the detection figures have to be read against their reference standard. The denominator of 891 lesions is the union of lesions seen on any of the three tests, which structurally pushes the most sensitive modality toward 100% and the others downward. In the 25 patients (19%) who were operated and so had histology, per-lesion true positives fell to 72 of 113 (63.7%) for the PET, 44 of 113 (38.9%) for CT or MRI and 25 of 113 (22.1%) for SPECT/CT - and all 38 histologically proven lesions missed by every imaging test were nodal metastases. Only 110 of the 891 lesions were pancreatic, the cohort was enriched for MEN1 and VHL by inclusion criterion, change in management was adjudicated unblinded by the team that ordered the scans, and there are no follow-up or outcome data. Receptor PET is not a surveillance test: NCCN states that somatostatin-receptor imaging and FDG-PET are not recommended for routine surveillance, and the SNMMI/EANM standard adds that a rise or fall in lesional uptake must not be read as response or progression the way it would be with other tracers. [EXPERTISE]

standard.t: Record the main pancreatic duct calibre, any calcification and whether the lesion is cystic — all three carry information that size does not.
standard.pref: Every lesion being considered for observation. In 981 patients resected for well-differentiated tumours at eight centres, calcification was present in 122 of 697 assessable patients (18%) and a predominantly cystic appearance in 120 of 702 (17%). Calcified tumours were larger (3.2 against 2.0 cm, p=0.001) and more often had Ki-67 of 3% or more (47% against 33%, p=0.029), lymphovascular invasion (42% against 27%, p=0.005), nodal metastasis (36% against 24%, p=0.011), distant metastasis (13% against 4%, p<0.001) and metastasis on preoperative imaging (17% against 7%, p=0.001). Cystic tumours were less often node positive (12% against 30%, p<0.001). Five-year recurrence-free survival was 66% with calcification against 79% without (p=0.002) and 83% for cystic against 73% for solid (p=0.033); in the four-way comparison it was 91% for cystic without calcification (n=89), 77% for solid without calcification (n=494), 69% for solid with calcification and 67% for cystic with calcification (n=16), p=0.043. A dilated duct is the ASPEN study's single strongest stated warning sign.
standard.avoid: Do not call a calcified lesion low risk because it measures 1.4 cm, and do not treat a dilated duct as incidental - see the flagged disagreement at gate 4. Equally, do not convert either feature into a threshold. This is information for the board to weigh alongside grade and growth, not a rule.
standard.note: Grade D, downgraded on the full-text read. Calcification's independent hazard ratio was 11.5 with a 95% confidence interval of 1.1 to 125.0 at p=0.043, in a Cox model that also returned 25.2 (4.4-142.9) for nodal and 33.0 (4.4-249.3) for distant metastasis - the signature of far too few recurrence events for the covariates entered, with no event count reported anywhere in the paper. Cystic morphology, one of its two headline features, was not independently prognostic at all (HR 1.6, 0.2-14.3, p=0.69), although the abstract presents both as usable for stratification. Imaging was classified from radiology report wording rather than by central re-read, across eight institutions and seventeen years of changing technique; 28-29% of the cohort has no data on the two exposures of interest and the analysis is complete-case with no imputation; median follow-up was 35 months in a disease that recurs at a median of 4 to 7 years; the cystic-and-calcified cell that anchors the four-way comparison contains 16 patients; and no patient in the cohort was observed, which the authors concede before recommending the features for the observation decision anyway.

alt.t: Where a G2 or higher tumour has had both a receptor PET and an FDG-PET, record and report the pair together - a discordant result carries prognostic information that grade alone does not.
alt.pref: The NETPET grade summarises the pair on the single lesion that is most FDG-avid relative to its receptor uptake, plus the burden of such lesions. In the 62-patient derivation cohort, median overall survival was not reached for receptor-positive, FDG-negative disease (P1) or for the mixed group (P2-4) and was 11 months for significant FDG-positive, receptor-negative disease (P5), p=0.0018. In a 319-patient three-centre cohort, median overall survival was 101.8, 46.5 and 11.5 months and median time to progression 25.5, 16.7 and 6.6 months across the same three strata (both p<0.001), with the score independent of histological grade on multivariable analysis (HR 2.376, 95% CI 1.682-3.357, p<0.001) and grade independent of the score (HR 1.615, 1.192-2.187, p=0.002). Inter-rater kappa was 0.8 and intra-rater kappa 0.9.
alt.avoid: Do not use this to decide an operation on a localised primary. Both cohorts were metastatic or unresectable disease; only 39% and 36% of patients had pancreatic primaries and no pancreas-specific subgroup is reported in either; two of the three validation centres supplied the original derivation data, so this is partly a re-analysis rather than external validation; and treatment was not modelled in either paper, which matters because receptor-positive, FDG-negative disease is precisely the eligibility criterion for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, so part of the P1 advantage is access to an effective drug. The 5-point scale has never been shown to be prognostic level by level - every published analysis collapses it to three categories, and several sub-grades contained a single patient. The score carries no treatment threshold.
alt.note: The SNMMI/EANM procedure standard makes the same point more cautiously: FDG positivity is not rare in G1 and G2 tumours and predicts progression and prognosis more strongly than tumour grade, and combining the two scans can identify the highest-grade, most aggressive lesion and direct a biopsy to it. What no source gives is what to do with the result in a localised primary. See the honest section. [EXPERTISE]

avoid.t: Do not operate on uncinate-process or tail uptake seen on a somatostatin-receptor PET without a lesion on dedicated pancreas-protocol CT or MRI.
avoid.pref: When pancreatic uptake is seen, obtain pancreas-protocol contrast CT to establish whether there is an underlying lesion at all.
avoid.avoid: Physiological pancreatic uptake is described in over half of patients imaged with receptor PET, there is substantial overlap between physiological and malignant activity, and uptake alone cannot characterise a pancreatic finding. The SNMMI/EANM procedure standard says the same and goes no further: physiologically increased uptake in the pancreatic head and uncinate process occurs in a large proportion of patients and overlaps substantially with the standardised uptake values of true lesions in that region, and the standard offers no decision rule beyond correlating with multiphase CT or MRI and following the patient up. Receptor PET also cannot distinguish a splenule or an intrapancreatic splenule from a small tumour - both take up as avidly as spleen - and should not be used to try.

avoid.t: Do not use somatostatin-receptor imaging to stage a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma as a matter of routine.
avoid.pref: Multiphasic CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis, with brain imaging and FDG-PET as appropriate, is the staging package NCCN sets for this disease.
avoid.avoid: NCCN states that receptor-based imaging is not part of the routine evaluation of poorly differentiated carcinoma. A negative receptor scan in that setting answers a question nobody needed to ask and delays treatment that is time-critical.

gates.name: 3 · The functional syndrome, and what it changes
crit: Insulinoma — neuroglycopenic symptoms with raised insulin, pro-insulin and C-peptide during concurrent hypoglycaemia
Gastrinoma — Zollinger-Ellison syndrome with a raised fasting gastrin, interpreted against proton-pump inhibitor use
Glucagonoma — glucagon excess with diabetes or necrolytic migratory erythema
VIPoma — watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia and achlorhydria with a raised VIP
Any other documented syndrome: somatostatinoma, ACTHoma, PTHrPoma, calcitoninoma, GHRHoma
gates.ask: Which hormone am I treating, where exactly is the tumour, and does the syndrome change the operation or only the preparation for it?

standard.t: A localised, biochemically confirmed functional tumour is resected, whatever its size — the syndrome is the indication and the 2 cm rule does not apply here.
standard.pref: Every localised functional tumour without distant metastases, where resection serves both symptom control and cure. Malignant potential runs from 5–15% for insulinoma to 60–90% for gastrinoma, glucagonoma and tumours secreting VIP, PTHrP or ectopic ACTH, so for everything except insulinoma the operation is an oncologic one. Resection of a localised insulinoma gives a 98% biochemical cure rate with a 6% chance of recurrence at 10 years.
standard.avoid: Do not apply the small-nonfunctional observation rule to a functional tumour. NCCN's resection requirement for glucagonoma, VIPoma and somatostatinoma is total removal with negative margins, including adjacent organs where involved, with regional nodes — pancreatoduodenectomy for the head, distal pancreatectomy with or without splenectomy for body and tail.
standard.note: Biochemical cure for apparently sporadic gastrinoma is 60% immediately after resection and 30-40% at 5 years, with 15-year disease-free survival of 15%, so "cured" means something different in each syndrome and should be said in those terms. For gastrinoma the strongest datum for operating is not randomised: on prospective NIH, UCSF and Stanford protocols, 160 patients who had a standardised exploration were compared with 35 who met the same criteria but did not have surgery. A gastrinoma was found and removed in 150 of 160 (94%), 51% were disease-free immediately and 41% at last follow-up. Liver metastases developed in 8 of 160 (5%) against 10 of 35 (29%), p=0.0002; death from any cause in 34 of 160 (21%) against 19 of 35 (54%), p=0.0002; disease-related death in 2 of 160 (1%) against 8 of 35 (23%), p=0.00001; and 15-year disease-related survival from first admission was 98% against 74%. Those 35 controls were not randomly formed - 19 refused after consulting their own physician, 10 had MEN1 with no lesion above 2.5 cm and 5 had comorbidity - non-disease mortality was numerically higher in them (31% against 20%, p=0.18), the surgical arm's disease-related figure rests on 2 deaths, cause of death was adjudicated unblinded by the operating investigators, and the controls were imaged every 6 to 12 months against yearly evaluation in the operated patients. Almost every primary was duodenal or nodal, so none of this transfers to an incidental non-functional pancreatic tumour. See the honest section and approval 4.

standard.t: Confirm the syndrome biochemically before localising, and read gastrin against the proton-pump inhibitor.
standard.pref: Serum gastrin ideally drawn fasting and off a proton-pump inhibitor for more than a week. Where there are overt clinical symptoms of gastrinoma or a risk of complications, NCCN says to continue the acid suppression and interpret the gastrin with that in mind rather than stop it. Consider endocrinology involvement to establish the endocrine diagnosis.
standard.avoid: Do not start a localisation workup on a gastrin drawn on a proton-pump inhibitor and do not stop acid suppression in a patient who is symptomatic or at risk of perforation or bleeding to obtain a cleaner number. Genetic counselling and testing is recommended for every gastrinoma — see gate 7.

standard.t: For insulinoma, enucleate an exophytic lesion that is clear of the main pancreatic duct; take a spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy for a deep lesion or one close to the duct.
standard.pref: Insulinomas are highly symptomatic and rarely malignant, which is exactly the setting in which NCCN and NANETS place enucleation. Ninety per cent pursue an indolent course. Where splenic vessels are involved by a larger tumour, splenectomy is performed; otherwise spleen preservation should be considered.
standard.avoid: Do not enucleate a lesion within 2-3 mm of the main pancreatic duct, and do not enucleate a tumour large enough to carry nodal risk - see gate 5 for the trade. And cost the fistula honestly: in a pooled analysis of 22 non-randomised comparative studies (432 enucleations against 716 standard resections), pancreatic fistula occurred in 25.5% after enucleation against 19.7% after standard resection, OR 2.09 (95% CI 1.41-3.11), p<0.001, and OR 1.93 (1.14-3.27) for clinically relevant grade B or C disease; the excess lost significance only in the four studies performing more than 20 enucleations in total and at least 4 a year. Vaccinate against pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae b and meningococcus at least 14 days before any operation that might include splenectomy.
standard.note: A formal lymphadenectomy is not part of the operation for a benign insulinoma.

alt.t: Where contrast CT or MRI and endoscopic ultrasound have not found the insulinoma, the next test is GLP-1 receptor imaging or arterial stimulation with venous sampling, not another anatomic study.
alt.pref: In a prospective randomised crossover study at one centre, 52 consecutive adults with biochemically proven endogenous hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia had 68Ga-DOTA-exendin-4 PET/CT, 111In-DOTA-exendin-4 SPECT/CT and a standardised 3T MRI within 3 to 4 days, each read independently by three blinded readers, with surgery, histology and postoperative glucose normalisation as the reference standard. Among the 38 who reached surgery with conclusive histology, accuracy was 93.9% (95% CI 87.8-97.5) for GLP-1 receptor PET/CT, 67.5% (58.1-76.0) for the SPECT, 67.6% (58.0-76.1) for the study MRI and 40.0% (23.9-57.9) for the prior external CT or MRI (all comparisons p<0.01 except SPECT against study MRI, p=1.0); reader agreement was 89.5%, 75.7% and 71.1%. Histology confirmed a benign insulinoma in 36 of 38 at a median size of 12 mm (range 5-23) and 37 of 38 normalised their glucose after surgery. ENETS recommends GLP-1 receptor imaging or arterial calcium stimulation with venous sampling when contrast CT or MRI and endoscopic ultrasound are negative.
alt.avoid: Read the accuracy figures for what they are. Fourteen of the 52 enrolled patients are absent from that denominator precisely because imaging was negative or discordant or surgery was declined, which is the classic verification bias of an imaging study with a surgical reference standard and which the authors concede inflates sensitivity - the PET showed a suspicious lesion in only 78.8% of all 52 patients. Inclusion required a pathological fasting test, so specificity and negative predictive value cannot be estimated at all. The 40% figure for prior external imaging is an artefact of why these patients were referred, not a general estimate, and that arm was read once at the referring centre against three blinded readers for the index test. GLP-1 receptor expression falls to 4 of 11 (36%) in malignant insulinoma, where 73% express somatostatin receptor 2 instead, so a negative exendin scan in a patient who looks malignant is uninformative. The tracer is not licensed for routine clinical use.
alt.note: The supporting review is a narrative one by the group that developed, labelled and validated the tracer, with no systematic search, no risk-of-bias appraisal and a comparative sensitivity table that places studies with different reference standards, referral filters and lesion sizes side by side. It does record the practical traps worth knowing: physiological uptake in duodenal Brunner's glands is always present and can be mistaken for an insulinoma, and high renal uptake can mask a lesion in the tail. [EXPERTISE]

alt.t: Where the lesion is resectable but the patient is not a surgical candidate, EUS-guided ablation at a centre with expertise is an option for insulinoma.
alt.pref: NCCN lists this for highly selected cases only. Stabilise first with diet, diazoxide at 3 to 8 mg/kg per day in three or four divided doses, or everolimus.
alt.avoid: This is a symptom-control manoeuvre with no comparative outcome data in this disease and no established oncologic endpoint. Do not offer it to an operable patient. [EXPERTISE]
alt.note: Correct the metabolic consequences of the syndrome before operating: potassium, magnesium and bicarbonate and dehydration in a VIPoma, glucose in an insulinoma. Glucagonoma carries a described hypercoagulable state and NCCN allows consideration of perioperative anticoagulation.

avoid.t: Do not give a somatostatin analogue to a patient with insulinoma whose somatostatin-receptor imaging is negative.
avoid.pref: Only consider an analogue in insulinoma where the tumour demonstrably expresses somatostatin receptors, and use it with caution even then because it can transiently worsen hypoglycaemia.
avoid.avoid: Analogues suppress the counter-regulatory hormones — growth hormone, glucagon and catecholamines — and in a receptor-negative insulinoma can precipitously worsen hypoglycaemia with fatal complications reported. About two-thirds of insulinomas are receptor-PET negative, so this is a common trap rather than a rare one, and it is why the receptor scan is obtained before the drug.

avoid.t: Do not rely on prophylactic octreotide to prevent an intraoperative crisis.
avoid.pref: Have vasopressors and fluid immediately available and give them without waiting. The crisis plan, the rescue drug in the room and the carcinoid-heart-disease assessment are set out in the NELM pathway's functional-syndrome gate, which applies unchanged to a patient coming for a pancreatic operation.
avoid.avoid: NCCN states that prophylactic octreotide is likely ineffective in preventing intraoperative carcinoid crisis and that intraoperative administration should not delay vasopressor use and fluid administration. NANETS calls the role of analogues in preventing crisis in pancreatic NET undefined. Also remember cholecystectomy at the index operation where long-term analogue therapy is anticipated, because of the raised risk of biliary symptoms and cholecystitis.

gates.name: 4 · The incidental small nonfunctional tumour: observe or resect
crit: Incidentally discovered, sporadic and non-functional, with no hormonal syndrome
2 cm or smaller on the index multiphasic CT or MRI, and low grade
No radiological nodal or distant disease, no vascular invasion
Main pancreatic duct not dilated
A patient who will actually come back for imaging, with the surgical risk and comorbidity burden stated
gates.ask: This patient has a 14 mm lesion in the pancreatic body found on a CT for something else — do I operate, or do I scan again in six months?

standard.t: Observation is the default for an incidental, low-grade, non-functional tumour of 1 cm or less, and biopsy is not required to make that decision.
standard.pref: A sub-centimetre lesion with the imaging phenotype of a neuroendocrine tumour in a patient who will be followed. At 1 cm the guidelines agree: NCCN permits observation for small, low-grade, incidentally discovered non-functional tumours and routes 1 cm or less straight to observation; NANETS calls initial observation without a plan for immediate resection an acceptable strategy for an asymptomatic tumour under 1 cm; and ENETS 2023, now read in full, states that an asymptomatic nonfunctioning tumour of 1 cm or less without main pancreatic duct dilation should undergo active surveillance (level 3 evidence, grade B).
standard.avoid: Do not observe a patient who will not return for imaging, and do not observe a lesion you have not characterised on a dedicated pancreas-protocol study. Observation is a programme with dates, not a decision to do nothing. And do not state, as the first draft of this page did from the abstract, that ENETS considers observation for lesions no larger than 2 cm. It does not. ENETS observes 1 cm or less, personalises the band above 1 cm up to 2 cm to the resection that would be required and the patient's comorbidities, and strongly recommends surgery for any nonfunctioning tumour larger than 2 cm or with main pancreatic duct dilation - all three positions at level 3 evidence, grade B.
standard.note: Grade D, downgraded on the full-text read. Neither 1 cm nor 2 cm was derived from data. NCCN's own supporting citations for the observation footnote are the three cohorts in the next item and nothing stronger; ENETS's surgical thresholds carry level 3 evidence while its strongest wording is reserved for the threshold above which it operates; and the only systematic comparison of surgery against surveillance for lesions of 2 cm or less that exists anywhere - 37 of 3,048 screened publications, 1,814 patients, carried out for the 2025 MEN1 recommendations - found no difference in metastasis or mortality, at low to very low GRADE certainty. The recommendation to observe a sub-centimetre lesion is reasonable and near-universal. It is not derived, and it should not be offered to a patient as though it were.

standard.t: State the actual evidence for the threshold when you offer observation: three uncontrolled cohorts with two to four years of follow-up, no randomised comparison, and not one direct comparison of the two strategies in any of them.
standard.pref: Every observation conversation, and every tumour board that uses the 2 cm line. The three studies NCCN cites are these, as their full texts report them. Sadot 2016 is a single-centre matched case-control study at one tertiary referral centre, 1993-2013, of sporadic incidentally discovered stage I-II tumours, and its inclusion band was 3 cm or less rather than 2 cm: median size was 1.2 cm (IQR 0.8-1.7) in the observed group and 1.4 cm (1-2) in the resected, and 87% were T1. Of 464 patients reviewed, 104 recommended for observation were matched one-to-one on initial tumour size by a blinded statistician to 77 resected without a period of surveillance, and compared by intention to treat. Median tumour size in the observation group was unchanged at 1.2 cm from first to last imaging (p=0.7) - but the individual trajectories differed: 53 of 104 (51%) grew, 19 (18%) were static and 32 (31%) shrank. Twenty-six of 104 (25%) crossed over to resection at a median of 30 months (range 7-135), for patient preference in 10 (38%), increasing size in 8 (31%), physician preference in 7 (27%) and new duct dilatation in 1 (4%); none had developed symptoms. No observed patient developed radiographic locoregional or distant metastases and nobody in either arm died of disease. In the resected arm 72 of 77 (95%) were G1, 1 was node positive, margins were positive in 9 (12%), and 5 (6%) recurred at a median of 5.1 years (range 2.9-8.1). Operative harm was substantial: any grade 3 complication in 16 of 77 (21%), a grade 3 leak-related complication in 13 (17%), median stay 7 days. PANDORA is the Dutch Pancreatic Cancer Group's nationwide prospective watchful-waiting cohort of 76 patients with a non-functional tumour of 2 cm or less, enrolled 2017-2020, median follow-up 17 months (IQR 8-35). Sixty-eight of 76 (89%) showed no sign of progression; 8 (11%) grew by more than 0.5 cm per year, of whom 2 ended above 2.0 cm, and none of the 8 developed symptoms. Six patients (8%) were operated during follow-up. One of them, who grew from 1.8 to 2.6 cm in a year, had two enlarged nodes on 68Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT and an unexpected peritoneal deposit at operation: final pathology was a 2.0 cm tumour with Ki-67 5-10%, two positive nodes and confirmed peritoneal metastasis, with two new nodes 11 months later requiring a somatostatin analogue. Four patients died, all of non-tumour causes. ASPEN is the largest: a prospective, non-randomised, international cohort of 500 patients at 41 centres, 406 under surveillance and 94 resected, with treatment left to the referring centre, median follow-up 25 months (IQR 16-35). Mean radiological size was 13.2 mm (SD 4.1) - 12.9 mm under surveillance against 14.8 mm in the surgical group, p<0.010. Nine of 406 surveillance patients (2%) came to surgery during follow-up: 4 for increasing size, 3 for increasing duct dilatation, 2 by preference. Distant metastases were present in 4 of 500 (0.8%), all at diagnosis and all operated, and the only recurrence recorded during follow-up was in one of those same patients. Severe complications occurred in 13% of the resected with no deaths.
standard.avoid: Do not present any of this as proof of safety, and do not present it as a comparison of strategies, because not one of the three performs one. Sadot's inclusion criterion was under 3 cm, so the paper most often cited for the 2 cm threshold never tested that threshold; its evidence concerns lesions of about a centimetre and it is silent about the 2-3 cm range it nominally covers. A quarter of its observation arm had the very operation the paper argues can be avoided, and they remain in that arm by intention to treat, so part of the arm's clean oncological record was purchased with surgery. The patients genuinely never operated were followed a median of 33 months (IQR 11-72) against 57 months after resection (p<0.001), while the recurrences in the resected arm appeared at a median of 5.1 years - the observation arm was not watched long enough to experience the event the paper reports as absent. The metastasis-free survival advantage for observation, 99% (97-100) against 88% (79-96), p=0.01, is an artefact of the endpoint and not a finding: a resected patient can be recorded as recurring while an unresected patient with stable imaging cannot, so the two arms are not at risk of the same events, and in the observation-only against resection comparison the difference disappears (metastasis-free survival p=0.08, overall survival p=0.3). Matching was on initial size alone: the observation group was significantly older (median 63 against 59, p=0.04; 65 against 59 in the never-operated subgroup, p=0.001), 36 of 104 (35%) never had a tissue diagnosis at all, and 11 of 181 (6%) died of other or unknown causes with no competing-risk analysis. Fifty-one per cent of observed tumours did grow, a fact submerged beneath an unchanged median. ASPEN's 20% rate of aggressive histology - its most quoted number - comes entirely from the 94 patients who were resected, and that group was selected by radiological size over 10 mm (OR 1.9, p=0.030), a main pancreatic duct over 3 mm (OR 3.4, p<0.001), age 64 or under (OR 2.5, p<0.001), enrolment at a surgical centre (OR 2.0, p=0.012) and a HADS anxiety score of 4-6 (OR 2.0, p=0.029). It therefore cannot describe the prevalence of aggressive biology among sub-2 cm lesions and certainly not among the 406 who were watched. Follow-up was 25 months in a disease measured in decades, crossover was 2%, allocation was by the treating centre rather than randomised, and no outcome comparison between the two strategies was performed at all. The metastasis rate is printed in the paper as 0.08 per cent when 4 of 500 is 0.8 per cent - a tenfold typographical understatement of the key safety signal, uncorrected. A third of patients never had a fine-needle aspirate and grade was not evaluable in a quarter of those who did, so the surveillance arm has no histological characterisation and the extent of under-staging in it is unmeasurable. The study was funded by ENETS, whose guideline recommending surveillance is the hypothesis under test, and senior authors wrote that guideline. In PANDORA, six of the eight patients who met the protocol's own criterion for resection refused the operation and elected to continue watchful waiting, so the protocol was in effect not tested and the cohort's benign course reflects patient choice. Protocol adherence was poor: only 17 of 76 (22%) had the scheduled 3-month endoscopic ultrasound, 19 (25%) had only one imaging modality at diagnosis against a protocol requiring two, and 21 (28%) and 11 (15%) had no imaging at all at 6 and 12 months. Eligibility excluded patients with malignant tumour features - exactly the population whose risk determines whether waiting is safe. And one lesion resected for diagnostic uncertainty proved to be an intravascular pyogenic granuloma and not a neuroendocrine tumour at all, which means some surveilled lesions may not be either.
standard.note: The nearest thing to a comparison of the two strategies is negative. The 2025 MEN1 best-practice exercise ran a systematic review of surgery against active surveillance for nonfunctioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours of 2 cm or less: across 37 of 3,048 screened publications - 27 retrospective series, 1 prospective cohort and 9 case series - covering 1,814 patients, combined metastatic disease and mortality rates did not differ between the two strategies, at low to very low GRADE certainty and with low precision. The panel notes that surgery in those series was indicated by growth on serial imaging, so the effect of surgery may be understated. That review is in MEN1, where the gland carries a field defect, lesions are multiple and patients are decades younger, so it does not transfer to sporadic disease - but it is the only systematic comparison in existence at this size, and it found nothing. The same panel then recommended a more cautious approach anyway, on expert judgement rather than on the evidence it had convened to produce, which is a defensible clinical position and should not be quoted as evidence-based.

standard.t: Set the surveillance programme in writing at the moment observation is chosen, using the post-resection schedule.
standard.pref: NCCN states that its surveillance recommendations apply to cases where observation has been chosen: history and examination with multiphasic abdomen with or without pelvis CT or MRI at 12 weeks to 12 months, then every 6 to 12 months to a maximum of 10 years, then as clinically indicated, with chest CT as clinically indicated and earlier imaging if symptoms develop. Use the same modality and contrast agent each time so that growth is measurable rather than inferred - ENETS makes the same point explicitly, that imaging modality, contrast type, contrast timing and tracer should not be changed during follow-up.
standard.avoid: Receptor-based imaging and FDG-PET are not recommended for routine surveillance. Do not let the interval drift: the trigger for resection in every one of the three cohorts above was measurable growth, which only exists if the measurements are comparable.
standard.note: Grade D, and the borrowed schedule is now known to disagree with its own source. The published follow-up recommendations for completely resected gastroenteropancreatic tumours - a 22-member RAND/UCLA panel scoring 193 scenarios against an evidence base of 6 eligible studies plus two then-unpublished cohorts - recommend for a resected pancreatic tumour consultation with triple-phase CT or MRI yearly for 3 years, then every 1 to 2 years to a total of 10 years, deliberately de-intensifying the first three years relative to NCCN, ENETS, ESMO and NANETS while extending surveillance past ten. They also recommend no follow-up at all for a grade 1, node-negative pancreatic tumour smaller than 2 cm. That exemption is expert opinion at a 75% agreement threshold, in a dataset whose cumulative recurrence was 33.5% at 5 years and 48.5% at 10 and whose median time to pancreatic recurrence was 7.2 years, and node-negative in a small tumour usually means few or no nodes were taken. It applies to resected patients and not to observed ones, and this page does not adopt it - but the group should know that the schedule it borrows is contradicted by the paper it is borrowed from. ENETS 2023 sets a third schedule again, imaging at 3 to 6 months after curative resection, then every 6 to 12 months for 5 years, every 12 to 24 months to 10 years and then every 5 years, at level 5 evidence graded B, with patients told to expect at least 20 years and possibly lifelong surveillance. See approval 13.

alt.t: Define in advance what counts as growth, record a rate rather than a size, and say plainly that no growth threshold in use has been derived.
alt.pref: Two thresholds are in circulation and the board should pick one and write it down. PANDORA used growth of more than 0.5 cm per year as its protocol trigger, and 8 of 76 patients (11%) met it at a median of 17 months. The 2025 MEN1 recommendations use growth of under 1 mm per year as the point at which the imaging interval may be lengthened to every 1 to 2 years, at 92% panel agreement, with intervals individualised to the observed growth rate and the absolute size. In ASPEN, increasing size was the stated indication for surgery in only 4 of the 406 surveillance patients, against patient preference in 42 of 94 operated patients and centre preference in 37.
alt.avoid: Do not present either number as biological - neither has any cited derivation. One millimetre a year lies below the measurement reproducibility of serial cross-sectional imaging of a small pancreatic lesion across different scanners and readers, and will generate both false stability and false progression. Half a centimetre a year is no better founded: in PANDORA the 8 patients who met it had a mean size at last follow-up of still only 1.2 cm (SD 0.7), and only 2 of them ever crossed 2.0 cm, so the threshold was detecting measurement variation as much as growth. What makes either threshold usable at all is the same modality, the same contrast agent and the same measurement convention every time, which is the one part of this that is entirely within the programme's control.
alt.note: Record the measurement in the body of the note, in millimetres, naming the phase and sequence it was made on. A growth rate that cannot be recomputed from the chart is not a growth rate. See approval 12.

avoid.t: Do not treat 2 cm as a biological boundary.
avoid.pref: Use it as the point at which the conversation changes, and decide with grade, growth rate, duct calibre, calcification, location, age and comorbidity.
avoid.avoid: The number does not survive a receiver-operating-characteristic analysis: in 5,172 SEER patients with pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms, 1,760 of them 2 cm or less, the cutoff best associated with aggressive behaviour was 2.50 cm - area under the curve 0.769 (95% CI 0.755-0.782), sensitivity 81.3%, specificity 63.3% - and in that same dataset a size of 1-2 cm against 1 cm or less was not prognostic for overall survival (HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.65-1.31, p=0.652) while it did predict who was offered an operation (OR 1.60, 1.20-2.12, p=0.001). Below the line, metastatic potential is real rather than absent: 4 of 500 ASPEN patients (0.8%) had distant metastases at diagnosis. And in the National Cancer Data Base, among 1,854 non-functional tumours of 2 cm or less, 303 (29%) presented with regional nodal metastases and 180 (10%) with distant metastases, with nodal involvement failing to fall at the smallest sizes - 33% among the 94 tumours of 0.5 cm or less - while distant metastasis did rise with size (10.5% at 0.5 cm or less, 8.5% at 0.5-1.0 cm, 14.2% at 1-2 cm, p=0.02). Nodal risk may also not be uniform across populations: see the honest section and approval 3.
avoid.note: Do not read any of these in the other direction either. None of them shows that resecting a small tumour saves a life, and each carries a defect that points the same way. The 33% nodal figure for tumours of 5 mm or less rests on a band of 94 patients, in a variable missing in 45% of that cohort, with no confidence interval given; and the National Cancer Data Base by design records only tumours assigned a malignant behaviour code, which removes exactly the indolent small lesions a surveillance policy is about, so 29% and 10% are a ceiling for a selected malignant subset rather than estimates for an incidental lesion. The paper's own authors say the registry may overestimate the malignant potential of small tumours, and it carries no Ki-67, no mitotic rate and no disease-specific survival. The SEER cutoff of 2.50 cm was derived and reported in the same dataset with no validation, against a composite "aggressiveness" outcome assembled from poor differentiation, nodal involvement, liver involvement and advanced stage - variables mathematically entangled with size and with each other, so size was guaranteed to predict the composite - and a specificity of 63% would be unusable at the bedside. In that same analysis, surgery was associated with better overall survival both before and after propensity matching while cancer-specific survival was comparable after matching, which is the signature of confounding by comorbidity rather than a treatment effect: SEER cannot distinguish a patient enrolled in planned surveillance from one never offered an operation, and before matching that arm was older (65 or over in 52.8% against 36.1%) with seven times the rate of liver involvement (7.0% against 1.0%). There is no imaging follow-up, no growth rate and no crossover anywhere in it, so despite its title it has no purchase on surveillance as a strategy.

avoid.t: Do not let an observation decision be made without naming who owns the next scan and when it is due.
avoid.pref: One owner, one date, one named modality, recorded in the board output. A patient told "we will keep an eye on it" is not under surveillance.
avoid.avoid: In ASPEN, patient preference was the stated reason for surgery in 42 of 94 cases (45%) and centre preference in 37 (39%) - 84% between them - duct dilatation in 11 (12%) and distant metastases in 4 (4%); a HADS anxiety score of 4-6 was independently associated with operating (OR 2.0, p=0.029) and enrolment at a surgical centre doubled the odds (OR 2.0, p=0.012). Unowned surveillance converts into an operation driven by accumulated anxiety and local culture rather than by tumour behaviour. The PANDORA quality-of-life finding is about the moment of entry rather than the experience of waiting: at baseline, patients scored worse than the reference population for emotional functioning (83.9 against 89.0, p=0.042), insomnia (22.9 against 14.0, p=0.046), dyspnoea (18.8 against 7.1, p=0.004) and nausea and vomiting (6.9 against 2.7, p=0.037), and its authors call the result too premature to interpret. Either way the psychological cost is measurable at the start of surveillance and should be addressed there rather than absorbed - three of PANDORA's six operations had no protocol indication at all, two of them for fear of progression and one because the surgeon did not support watchful waiting.

gates.name: 5 · Which operation for a resectable tumour
crit: Nonfunctional tumour larger than 2 cm, or invasive, or node-positive on imaging
Malignant-appearing tumour of any size
A functional tumour that has been localised
A 1–2 cm tumour where the board has decided to resect
Patient fit for the operation that the tumour's position actually requires
gates.ask: Does this tumour need a formal oncologic resection, or can I take it out and leave the patient their pancreas?

standard.t: Standard oncologic surgery — distal pancreatectomy with or without splenectomy, or pancreatoduodenectomy — is the operation for most resectable non-metastatic tumours.
standard.pref: Tumours larger than 2 cm, malignant-appearing tumours, and functional tumours other than insulinoma. For a tumour larger than 2 cm or malignant-appearing, NCCN requires total removal with negative margins including adjacent organs where involved, together with regional nodes: pancreatoduodenectomy for the head, distal pancreatectomy with or without splenectomy or a spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy for body and tail.
standard.avoid: Do not choose the operation from the size alone — position relative to the main pancreatic duct and the nodal question decide it. Splenectomy is generally included, but spleen preservation should be considered for a benign insulinoma; vaccinate at least 14 days before where splenectomy is possible.
standard.note: Outcome context from the largest resected series, 3,851 patients in the National Cancer Data Base, 1985-2004: 5-year overall survival 59.3% and 10-year 37.7%, relative survival 65.7% and 47.8%, median follow-up 51 months. The independent predictors were age (55-75 HR 1.57, 95% CI 1.28-1.91; over 75 HR 3.04, 2.17-4.25), a nonfunctional tumour (HR 1.45, 1.06-1.97), high-grade histology (HR 2.03, 1.41-2.92), liver metastases (HR 1.71, 1.36-2.14) and other distant metastases (HR 3.78, 1.51-9.43), with pancreatoduodenectomy against distal pancreatectomy also adverse (HR 1.63, 1.03-2.57, p=0.04). Tumour size was not an independent predictor in any parameterisation, nor were nodal status (HR 1.18, 0.96-1.45, p=0.12), margins (gross positive HR 1.72, 0.95-3.12, p=0.08), chemotherapy, radiotherapy or hospital volume. Read the size result carefully before importing it into the observation decision: only 19% of that cohort's tumours were 2 cm or less, 171 tumours a pathologist had coded benign were excluded by design, grade was missing in 43.5% and size in about 22% with no sensitivity analysis, and the resulting prognostic score was derived and tested in the same 836 complete-case patients with a concordance index of 0.63 (0.59-0.67) - barely above the 0.5 of chance. The paper cannot be used to argue that size is irrelevant to whether to resect a 1 cm incidental lesion. The adverse coefficient for pancreatoduodenectomy is far more plausibly perioperative mortality and tumour location than an effect of the operation, which the authors concede while retaining it. [EXPERTISE]

standard.t: Aim for a negative margin, but do not extend the resection to get a wider one.
standard.pref: NANETS' position is that resection with negative margins should be the goal but that no data support more aggressive resection to obtain wider surgical margins in this disease, which is what makes enucleation legitimate in selected patients. In the 3,851-patient National Cancer Data Base series, margin status was not an independent predictor of survival on multivariable analysis - a grossly positive margin carried HR 1.72 (95% CI 0.95-3.12, p=0.08) - although univariately well or moderately differentiated tumours did far better than poorly differentiated ones (5-year survival 63.9% against 28.3%, p<0.0001).
standard.avoid: Do not use a 1 mm margin as a reason for a bigger operation. NANETS reports an 8-centre review of 1,020 resected patients in which R1 (margin 1 mm or less) occurred in 15% and 10-year recurrence-free survival fell to 47% from 63% (HR 1.8, p=0.02) while 10-year overall survival was unchanged at 71.1% against 71.8% (p=0.392), with grade, perineural invasion and vascular invasion significant for overall survival on multivariable analysis and margin status not. That series is not in this page's full-text depot and the figures are quoted as NANETS states them; the three-centre cohort that is in the depot reports R1 in 32 of 211 (15%), significant univariately and dropping out on backward selection.
standard.note: What does predict recurrence is biology. In 211 curatively resected G1 and G2 non-functional tumours at three high-volume European centres, followed a median of 51 months, 35 (17%) recurred at a median of 43 months (IQR 23-62), 91% of them within 5 years and 69% in the pancreatic remnant; 5- and 10-year disease-specific survival were 98% and 84% and overall survival 91% and 68%. The independent predictors of recurrence within 5 years were grade 2 (HR 4.07, 95% CI 1.87-8.84, p<0.001), positive lymph nodes (HR 2.44, 1.17-5.09, p=0.017) and perineural invasion (HR 2.38, 1.11-5.10, p=0.026); tumour size, R1 and vascular invasion were significant univariately and dropped out on backward selection. Of 107 patients with none of the three factors, 2 recurred. Operative harm in that cohort was substantial too: major complications in 58 of 211 (27%) and grade B or C pancreatic fistula in 46 (22%). All three score components are postoperative findings, so the instrument says nothing about whether to operate - see gate 9 for what it can and cannot do.

alt.t: Enucleation and central pancreatectomy are legitimate for a small, superficial tumour clear of the main duct - at a centre doing enough of them, and with the nodal question settled before the incision.
alt.pref: A tumour clear of the main pancreatic duct by more than 2 to 3 mm in a patient for whom preserving parenchyma matters. In a random-effects meta-analysis of 22 observational comparative studies (1,148 patients: 432 enucleations against 716 standard resections, 388 of them distal pancreatectomies and 328 pancreatoduodenectomies), enucleation gave less endocrine insufficiency (risk difference -0.08, 95% CI -0.12 to -0.04, p<0.001, I-squared 0%) and less exocrine insufficiency (-0.17, -0.31 to -0.04, p=0.01, I-squared 86%), 298 mL less blood loss (p<0.001), 78.4 minutes less operating time (p<0.001) and a stay shorter by 1.31 days (-2.55 to -0.06, p=0.04), with no difference in mortality (OR 1.49, 0.54-4.15), overall complications (OR 1.08, 0.68-1.73) or reoperation (OR 0.97, 0.46-2.04). ENETS adds the context: curative resection of a nonfunctioning tumour carries 5-year survival of 70-80%, and pancreatic resection carries morbidity up to 50% and mortality up to 3% even in high-volume centres.
alt.avoid: It costs fistula. Pancreatic fistula occurred in 25.5% after enucleation against 19.7% after standard resection, OR 2.09 (1.41-3.11), p<0.001, holding in the subset using the ISGPF definition (OR 2.15, 1.30-3.57) and for clinically relevant grade B or C disease (OR 1.93, 1.14-3.27, p=0.01, I-squared 0%). The excess lost significance only in the four studies performing more than 20 enucleations in total and at least 4 a year (OR 1.72, 0.87-3.38, p=0.12), which makes this a volume-conditional operation - see approval 5. And do not choose it to avoid a lymphadenectomy the tumour warrants: the review states plainly that it cannot address whether enucleation without lymphadenectomy is oncologically adequate, which is the question a surveillance pathway actually needs answered.
alt.note: Grade C. No randomised trial exists; all 22 studies were observational, mean methodological quality was 13 of a possible 27 on a modified Downs and Black checklist, only one of the 22 reported information on principal confounders, and only 4 performed more than 20 enucleations. The operations were chosen for anatomically different lesions and the review concedes it cannot tell whether the standard-resection patients were ever enucleation candidates, so part of every difference is lesion size and position rather than the operation. Indications pooled insulinoma, non-functioning tumours, serous and mucinous cystadenoma, IPMN and chronic pancreatitis, so no result is specific to a neuroendocrine tumour; the hospital-stay result is acknowledged to be driven by between-country practice; and the volume threshold was defined by the review's own authors and inserted into the quality checklist, so the least pre-specified analysis is the one carried into the conclusion. [EXPERTISE]

alt.t: Minimally invasive and robotic approaches are reasonable for distal pancreatectomy and in experienced hands for central pancreatectomy.
alt.pref: NCCN suggests considering minimally invasive resection for a distal insulinoma. For central pancreatectomy, a laparoscopic-versus-open comparison reported shorter stay, less blood loss, earlier return to diet and better long-term quality of life, and a randomised trial of robot-assisted versus open central pancreatectomy reported shorter stay, reduced operative time, less blood loss, a lower clinical fistula rate and faster recovery.
alt.avoid: Do not let the approach dictate the oncologic operation. A spleen-preserving laparoscopic distal pancreatectomy that cannot deliver the nodal count the tumour warrants is the wrong operation done elegantly. Neither of the central-pancreatectomy comparisons above is in this page's full-text depot; both are quoted as NANETS reports them, neither was powered for an oncologic endpoint, and ENETS notes separately that robust data on minimally invasive pancreatoduodenectomy in this disease are lacking. [EXPERTISE]

avoid.t: Do not use neoadjuvant therapy outside a trial or a specific downstaging intention.
avoid.pref: NANETS states that the efficacy of neoadjuvant therapy for resectable or borderline-resectable disease remains unclear and that randomised trials are needed, while allowing it as an option for downstaging selected patients with advanced or metastatic disease, especially before cytoreductive surgery — which is the NELM pathway's territory.
avoid.avoid: The supporting data are a retrospective MD Anderson series in which 29 of 356 patients with localised disease received 5-fluorouracil, doxorubicin and streptozocin, 48% went on to pancreatectomy and median overall survival was 112 months in the resected against 41 months in the unresected - a comparison of patients selected by their response. A propensity-matched NCDB study of 301 patients receiving perioperative systemic therapy against 301 having surgery alone found no difference for neoadjuvant therapy (P=0.21) and worse survival in the adjuvant group (P=0.037), with the agents not recorded. Neither series is in this page's full-text depot; both are quoted as NANETS and NCCN report them.

avoid.t: Do not book a pancreatoduodenectomy for a tumour you have not finished staging.
avoid.pref: Liver and nodal status, duct calibre and receptor status before the operating list, not after. A receptor PET that finds an occult liver deposit converts this into the NELM pathway and changes which operation — if any — is right.
avoid.avoid: NCCN's warning is explicit: a Whipple in metastatic disease is usually not curative and compromises later liver-directed therapy, and liver-directed therapy after a Whipple carries increased risk of cholangitis and liver abscess. That is an irreversible cost imposed on a patient whose disease is going to be managed hepatically for years.

gates.name: 6 · Lymphadenectomy — how many nodes, and when
crit: A formal pancreatoduodenectomy or distal pancreatectomy is planned
Tumour larger than 1.5 cm, or in the head of the pancreas
Ki-67 above 20%, or lymphovascular invasion on biopsy
Suspicious nodes on preoperative imaging or at exploration
A parenchyma-sparing operation is planned for a tumour of 2 cm or less
gates.ask: Am I taking nodes to stage this patient, to treat them, or because the operation happened to include them?

standard.t: Where a formal pancreatoduodenectomy or distal pancreatectomy is being done, retrieve 11 to 15 nodes for accurate nodal staging.
standard.pref: Every oncologic resection. The count is derived rather than tested, and it is not derived in this disease. NANETS reports that compared with 1-5 and 6-10 nodes, examining 11-15 raised the likelihood of finding a nodal metastasis 2.3-fold and 1.5-fold respectively, while 16-20 or more than 20 added nothing; the primary study behind that figure is not in this page's full-text depot, and NANETS itself states that unlike gastric and colon cancer there is no universally accepted minimum node number for prognostication here. With a standard pancreatoduodenectomy or a distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy the count is usually not difficult to achieve. ENETS 2023 draws the line differently again: routine lymphadenectomy for tumours over 3 cm and case-by-case for 2-3 cm, on the ground that no preoperative test accurately predicts nodal involvement.
standard.avoid: Do not present the node count as a therapeutic intervention. In the National Cancer Data Base series of 1,854 non-functional tumours of 2 cm or less, 999 of which were resected, 72.8% had a lymphadenectomy with a median of 8 nodes examined and 27% had no node examined at all; after adjustment there was no 2-year or 5-year survival difference between patients who did and did not have one, and no difference by type of resection (p=0.16). NANETS additionally reports a SEER analysis of 981 patients finding no survival advantage from sampling 10 or more nodes, a study not in this page's depot. The count is a staging instrument.
standard.note: Nodal status does carry prognostic weight, and the reading of it has to be exact. In 136 operated patients with locoregional disease at one unit, 133 of whom had nodes resected, 50 (37.6%) were node positive with a mean of 13.7 plus or minus 11.5 nodes retrieved, and median disease-free survival was 4.5 against 14.6 years (log-rank p<0.0001), with 5- and 10-year disease-free survival 48.2% and 32.1% against 86.8% and 70.8%. Overall survival did not reach significance: 77.1% and 55.4% against 91.3% and 74.6%, log-rank 0.1. The frequency of nodal metastasis rose with tumour size above 1.5 cm (OR 4.7, 95% CI 1.81-12.35, p=0.002), head location against body and tail (OR 2.8, 1.3-5.8, p=0.007), Ki-67 above 20% (OR 6.7, 1.6-27.3, p=0.008) and lymphovascular invasion (OR 3.6, 1.5-8.6, p=0.004) - but on multivariable analysis no variable independently predicted nodal metastasis at all, those odds ratios were fitted on incomplete and varying subsets (lymphovascular invasion known in 97 of 136, Ki-67 in 121, grade in 112), and median nodes examined were 15 for head against 8 for body and tail (p=0.0002), so part of the location effect is a detection effect. Grade D for the 11-to-15 target: a borrowed number supported by a study this page has not read, in a cohort where no preoperative variable independently predicted the thing the count is for.

standard.t: Where a parenchyma-sparing operation is planned for a tumour of 2 cm or less, remove any node that looks suspicious on imaging and consider sampling even when imaging is negative.
standard.pref: That is NANETS' recommendation verbatim, and the reason is that preoperative variables cannot exclude nodal disease. In the 136-patient series, multivariable analysis identified no independent predictor of nodal metastasis, and on the probability plot even the smallest pancreatic head tumours carried a nodal risk whose lower 95% bound sat just under 20%, with the smallest body and tail tumours estimated near 20% and a lower bound of 8.8%. Nodal metastasis was present in 2 of 17 tumours of 1 cm or less (12%) and 5 of 38 of 1.5 cm or less (13%). NANETS reports nodal metastasis in 12.9% to 27.3% of tumours of 2 cm or less, regardless of location.
standard.avoid: Do not treat a spleen-preserving or central resection as nodally adequate by default. For body and tail lesions that means attention to the hepatic artery, celiac axis and splenic artery nodes; for head lesions, the posterior pancreatic and portocaval nodes. Whether removing them changes survival has not been established. And read the low-risk estimates for what they are: 2 of 17 patients carries a confidence interval running from roughly 2% to 36%, which can neither support nor refute any size threshold, and every patient in that cohort was operated at a unit that states its own institutional bias toward complete oncological resection - so the favourable small lesions that would populate a low-risk tail are structurally absent from the dataset, which the authors acknowledge before drawing a management conclusion from it anyway.
standard.note: Nodal risk may not be uniform across populations. In a multi-institutional resected cohort from the US Neuroendocrine Tumor Study Group and a National Cancer Database validation cohort, nodal metastasis in tumours under 2 cm was 7 of 30 (23%) in Black patients against 8 of 151 (5%) in white patients, and 54 of 258 (21%) against 188 of 1,596 (12%), both p<0.01, with no racial difference in any larger size band; tumour size as a continuous variable predicted nodal metastasis in white patients only. The finding below 1 cm did not replicate - 2 of 8 (25%) against 0 of 33 (0%), p<0.01, in the first dataset but 7 of 67 (10%) against 31 of 354 (9%), p=0.66, in the validation. Every patient in both cohorts was resected with nodes removed, the two datasets overlap institutionally because the study group's own institutions report to the national database, grade was excluded from one and unavailable in the other, and no measure of insurance, income, referral delay or access to imaging was available. See the honest section and approval 3.

alt.t: A pragmatic position: take the nodes because it makes the next decision possible, not because it treats the cancer.
alt.pref: NANETS puts it this way — reducing tumour burden through lymphadenectomy, or at the very least removing suspicious nodes seen on imaging or at exploration, is likely to facilitate future management. Nodal metastasis is one of the three independent predictors in the published recurrence score, so a patient whose nodal status is unknown cannot be risk-stratified for surveillance intensity afterwards.
alt.avoid: Do not inflate this into a survival claim. The relationship between nodal metastasis and survival is genuinely inconsistent across series, and the reasons are structural: small numbers, inconsistent nodal sampling and pathological assessment, and follow-up too short for an indolent disease. NANETS reports a 326-patient cohort in which overall survival did not differ by nodal status at 2.7 years of follow-up and did differ significantly at 11 years; that paper is not in this page's depot. The one nodal cohort read in full here makes the same point in its own data and in the other direction: nodal status predicted disease-free survival strongly and overall survival not at all (log-rank 0.1), and its authors argue that the overall-survival result will become significant with longer follow-up rather than reporting the result they obtained, then use the disease-free finding to justify routine lymphadenectomy.

alt.t: Extended lymphadenectomy has no established place.
alt.pref: Take the regional basin that the standard operation delivers and stop there.
alt.avoid: No survival benefit of extended dissection has been established, and unlike gastric and colon cancer there is no universally accepted minimum node number for prognostication in this disease — the 11 to 15 figure is borrowed from the pancreatic adenocarcinoma literature.

avoid.t: Do not convert a planned enucleation into a Whipple intraoperatively to obtain nodes.
avoid.pref: Decide the operation, and therefore the nodal strategy, at the board and before the incision. If the nodal question is live enough to need a formal resection, plan one.
avoid.avoid: The extent of resection has not been shown to change survival in small non-functional tumours: in 1,854 National Cancer Data Base patients with tumours of 2 cm or less, unadjusted 5-year overall survival after excluding metastatic and medically inoperable patients was 83.0% (95% CI 74.0-89.1) after partial pancreatectomy, 72.3% (60.4-81.2) after pancreatoduodenectomy and 86.0% (66.8-94.5) after total pancreatectomy, and after adjustment there was no difference in the risk of death across surgery types (p=0.16) and none with or without regional lymphadenectomy. Escalating the operation in theatre spends morbidity on information.
avoid.note: Grade D. That survival analysis collapses 1,854 patients to 366 by requiring a diagnosis before 2006 and a known surgery type, nodes examined differed systematically by operation (63% of partial pancreatectomies against 89% of pancreatoduodenectomies and 75% of total pancreatectomies), and the registry records only tumours assigned a malignant behaviour code. The same analysis reports 27.6% 5-year survival with no surgery against 83.0% with partial pancreatectomy - a contrast between groups that differed in age (median 63 against 56-57), in poor differentiation (29.9% against 1.8-5.2%), in distant metastases (42.1% against 1.1-2.0%) and in treatment at an academic centre, which the authors concede in the discussion while retaining it in the abstract. It should not be quoted as an argument for operating. The same paper also reports a 15% relative reduction in the risk of death for each later calendar year of diagnosis during a window in which resection rates and metastasis rates did not change, which is far more plausibly stage migration from incidental detection than improving care.

gates.name: 7 · Hereditary syndromes — different thresholds, different timing
crit: Gastrinoma of the duodenum or pancreas, or a type 2 gastric NET
Multifocal pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours
Known or clinically suspected MEN1, MEN4, von Hippel-Lindau, NF1 or tuberous sclerosis
Primary hyperparathyroidism before age 30, multiple parathyroid adenomas, or recurrent hyperparathyroidism
A young patient, or a family history of any MEN1-associated tumour
gates.ask: Is this a sporadic tumour at all, and if it is not, which lesion in this pancreas am I actually operating on?

standard.t: Send for genetic evaluation rather than assuming a solitary tumour is sporadic.
standard.pref: NCCN recommends genetic risk evaluation and testing for gastrinoma, multifocal tumours, parathyroid disease before 30 or multigland disease, clinical suspicion of MEN1, and a mutation on tumour genomic testing with germline implications; it says to consider testing for a duodenal or pancreatic NET at any age. Studies of unselected patients have identified germline variants in 16% to 21% of cases, from relatively small cohorts.
standard.avoid: Do not let the result arrive after the operation. In MEN1 the lesion you can see is usually not the only lesion, and the finding changes the operation, its extent and its timing — not just the counselling.
standard.note: The MEN1 recommendations were comprehensively revised in 2025, and the revision read in full for this page produced 55 recommendations: 52 Delphi consensus statements from an expert panel in 22 countries, plus 3 from systematic reviews that found only 37 of 3,048 screened publications usable, covering 1,814 patients, with all three resulting recommendations rated low or very low certainty by GRADE. Use that document or the separate AACE consensus statement rather than a pre-2021 source for the surveillance schedule. The AACE statement is cited on this page from its abstract only - its full text was not obtained - so every numeric criterion attributed to it must be confirmed against the published paper before use.

standard.t: In MEN1, resect a functional tumour whatever its size, observe a nonfunctional tumour under 1 cm, and resect above 2 cm or on significant growth — accepting that surgery will not clear the gland.
standard.pref: NANETS: nonfunctional tumours under 1 cm can be observed and tumours over 2 cm should generally be resected; functional tumours should be removed where there is a dominant lesion. AACE 2025, from its abstract: functioning tumours resected regardless of size, nonfunctioning observed below 20 mm and strongly considered for resection above 20 mm or on significant growth under surveillance, with parenchyma-sparing surgery preferred. The 2025 best-practice recommendations say surgery should be considered for a growing nonfunctioning tumour and for one larger than 2 cm, with the indication settled by multidisciplinary discussion and shared decision making; ENETS 2023 observes 2 cm or less and advises resection above 2 cm (level 2, grade B), with 2-3 cm and any G2 tumour decided case by case. NCCN adds relatively rapid growth over 6 to 12 months as a third trigger alongside size and refractory symptoms. The threshold traces to a 108-patient cohort drawn from 579 registered MEN1 patients, in which nonfunctioning pancreatic tumours were the commonest pancreaticoduodenal lesion with a penetrance of 3% at age 20, 34% at 50 and 53% at 80, a mean size of 21 plus or minus 18 mm and a mean of 2.9 plus or minus 2.3 tumours per patient. Metastasis rose with size - 1 of 25 (4%) at 10 mm or less, 4 of 40 (10%) at 11-20 mm, 2 of 11 (18%) at 21-30 mm and 9 of 21 (43%) above 30 mm, Spearman 0.33, p<0.01 - and life expectancy was 68.5 years (95% CI 64-72.9) against 77.1 (74.4-79.9) for MEN1 patients without a pancreatic tumour, p<0.01. The authors concluded against routine surgery at or below 20 mm.
standard.avoid: Do not plan an operation intended to be definitive. Microadenomas make complete clearance unachievable, local intrapancreatic recurrence unrelated to margins is reported as high as 50%, and the residual pancreas and duodenum remain at risk because the predisposition does not go away - in that same cohort, 2 of 32 curatively resected patients were reoperated for new tumours. It remains unclear from the literature whether an extensive partial resection reduces malignant progression or prevents new tumours in the remnant.
standard.note: Grade D, downgraded on the full-text read. The 20 mm cut point was never derived: its two lowest strata are 1 of 25 and 4 of 40 patients whose confidence intervals overlap entirely, metastasis was imaging-defined in 60% of cases in a paper that itself cites evidence that a quarter of radiographically node-negative MEN1 patients have occult metastases at operation, mean follow-up after diagnosis was 4.3 plus or minus 3.3 years in a disease whose victims died at a mean age of 43, and the cohort spans 1956 to 2003 with prospective registration only from 1997, so penetrance and metastasis are estimated from different populations.
