The same paper's comparison of 32 curatively operated patients against 66 unoperated found no difference in metastasis (16% against 11%, p=0.5), death from the tumour (3.1% against 3%, p=0.99) or progression (22% against 12%, p=0.32) and no separation of the survival curves - an underpowered null, not evidence of equivalence, in groups that differed in follow-up and in mean size (30.2 against 16.3 mm, p=0.01). The 2025 systematic review reaches the same place from the other direction: across 37 studies and 1,814 patients, surgery and active surveillance for lesions of 2 cm or less produced no difference in metastasis or mortality at low to very low certainty. The 2025 recommendations add a surveillance schedule for a newly diagnosed lesion of 2 cm or less - repeat imaging at 6 to 12 months, again after 12 months if stable, then every 1 to 2 years if growth stays under 1 mm per year (92% agreement) - and a somatostatin-receptor PET for every patient planned for duodenopancreatic surgery (100% agreement). Hypergastrinaemia in MEN1 usually comes from small, multiple duodenal gastrinomas rather than from a pancreatic tumour, which is why NANETS allows medical management in many of these patients. Outcomes after surgery are good - 5-year overall survival 90-100% for functional and 65-100% for nonfunctional tumours - in a selected population. [EXPERTISE]

standard.t: In von Hippel-Lindau, use three factors rather than size alone: size 3 cm or more, doubling time under 500 days, and a germline exon 3 mutation.
standard.pref: NANETS: a patient with a tumour under 3 cm, doubling time over 500 days and a mutation outside exon 3 can be safely observed with imaging every 1 to 2 years; one high-risk factor means considering surgery or imaging at 6 to 12 month intervals; two or more means strongly considering resection. The derivation is a prospective NIH protocol in which 633 VHL patients were screened and 108 (17%) had a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour - none functional by hormone level or symptom - of whom 9 (8.3%) developed metastases and 2 died of them, 1.4% of everyone screened, over a median follow-up of 53 months. A primary larger than 3 cm was present in 6 of the 9 with metastases (67%) against 19 of 99 without (19%), p=0.0046; an exon 3 germline mutation in 7 of 9 (78%) against 32 of 98 (46%), p=0.01; and mean tumour doubling time was 337 days (range 180-463) against 2,628 days (103-9,614), p<0.0001. All 9 metastatic patients met at least two of the three criteria and 6 met all three, while among the 54 assessable patients without metastases 5 met two, 20 met one and 29 met none.
standard.avoid: Do not transfer the sporadic 2 cm threshold to VHL - the malignant potential is lower and the observation ceiling is correspondingly higher. Equally, do not assume every solid pancreatic lesion in a VHL patient is a neuroendocrine tumour: NANETS reports that about half of VHL patients develop benign pancreatic cysts, serous cystadenomas or haemangioblastomas, which need no intervention unless symptomatic or causing pancreatitis or biliary compression.
standard.note: Grade D, downgraded on the full-text read. The three-criterion rule was derived from 9 metastatic events and then declared to capture all 9, so its perfect sensitivity is a tautology of the derivation rather than a finding, with no independent or temporal validation attempted. Doubling time, the criterion with the largest apparent separation, was computable in all 9 metastatic patients but in only 54 of 99 without metastases, and patients with visibly growing lesions are imaged more often, so the exposure and the ability to measure it are entangled and 45 patients are simply absent from the stratification table. Sixty-nine of the 108 lesions were never resected and their diagnosis rests on CT or MRI appearance alone, which the senior author conceded in discussion could include microcystic adenomas. The 3 cm cut point was carried over from the group's own earlier publications and was never tested against 1 or 2 cm within the dataset - a discussant asked exactly that and was told the analysis had not been done - and the study dates are internally inconsistent between abstract and methods. There is no Ki-67, grade or differentiation datum anywhere in the series. Receptor PET is useful here specifically: differentiating a microcystic adenoma from a small tumour is difficult on CT and MRI in VHL, and receptor PET can resolve it. NANETS reports that these tumours cluster in the head and uncinate process (52%) against body (21%) and tail (28%).

alt.t: A somatostatin analogue is a reasonable antiproliferative option for MEN1-related tumours under 2 cm, on prospective but non-randomised evidence.
alt.pref: A MEN1 patient with one or more sub-2 cm tumours in whom the aim is to delay or avoid pancreatic surgery. In a prospective observational study at one Italian centre - 23 patients given lanreotide autogel 120 mg every 28 days and 19 continuing active surveillance, 91 lesions in all at a mean size of 6.8 plus or minus 3.4 mm, median follow-up 73 months (range 24-84) - median progression-free survival was not reached with lanreotide against 40 months under surveillance (p<0.001). On treatment there were 4 objective responses (17.4%), 15 stable (65.2%) and 4 progressing (17.4%); under surveillance 13 of 19 (68.4%) progressed and 6 (31.6%) were stable. Toxicity was minimal: one grade 1 diarrhoea and two cases of asymptomatic biliary stone disease, with no dose reduction or interruption.
alt.avoid: Treatment was chosen rather than allocated - lanreotide was proposed to every included patient as an alternative to surveillance - and the paper reports no comparison of comorbidity, disease burden, prior surgery or stated reason for the choice, so the arms differ by whatever disposes a patient to accept monthly injections for six years. The lanreotide arm also carried more tumours per patient at baseline (p=0.038), and patient-level progression-free survival is mixed with lesion-level response counting (22 of 62 treated lesions shrank against 0 of 29) with no adjustment for clustering of lesions within patients. Forty-two patients generated 17 radiological progression events in total, assessed unblinded with no central read, under a definition that counts a 20% size increase in a 7 mm lesion. Everything that matters was indistinguishable: liver metastases in 1 patient per arm, operations in 2 of 23 against 5 of 19, and no deaths. Do not extend it to sporadic small tumours, where there is no comparable evidence, no guideline support, and ENETS states explicitly that no evidence supports somatostatin analogues for controlling the progression of a small nonfunctioning tumour under surveillance.
alt.note: Grade D, downgraded on the full-text read. This is still the only prospective evaluation of analogues in MEN1-related tumours and it is cited by NCCN. The international consensus statement on the pancreas in MEN1 remains the fuller reference for how functioning and nonfunctioning duodenopancreatic disease is managed in this syndrome; it is cited on this page from its abstract only, its full text was not obtained, and the 2025 best-practice recommendations should be read alongside it.

alt.t: Belzutifan may be considered for a resectable tumour in a patient with a germline VHL alteration, individualised, and is not a substitute for an operation.
alt.pref: NCCN allows consideration of belzutifan for resectable tumours in germline VHL disease, with the decision individualised for small resectable lesions. The supporting trial is a phase 2, open-label, single-group study of 61 patients at 11 centres, all given belzutifan 120 mg daily, whose primary endpoint was objective response in renal cell carcinoma. After a median follow-up of 21.8 months the renal response rate was 49% (95% CI 36-62), all partial, with 24-month progression-free survival 96% (87-99). All 61 patients had pancreatic lesions, of which 47 (77%) responded including 6 complete responses; among the 22 patients who had pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours specifically, 20 (91%) had a confirmed response including 3 complete responses, at a median baseline target size of 21 mm (range 10-52) and a median time to response of 5.5 months. Central nervous system haemangioblastomas responded in 15 of 50 (30%). No patient underwent pancreatic surgery during the trial.
alt.avoid: Read the pancreatic figure for what it is: 20 of 22 patients, a secondary endpoint of a single-arm industry-sponsored trial with no comparator, no pre-specified statistical plan for it, no multiplicity control across the several organ systems assessed and no histological confirmation that each measured lesion was a neuroendocrine tumour rather than a serous cystadenoma - the two were deliberately measured together in the larger 77% figure. Eligibility required no renal tumour above 3 cm, no metastases and performance status 0 or 1, so the cohort is the fittest and least advanced end of the VHL population. Anaemia occurred in 90% of patients, grade 3 in 8%, with 20% needing erythropoiesis-stimulating agents and 7% transfusion, and fatigue in 66%; every patient's haemoglobin fell by at least 1.9 g/dL in the first 13 weeks. Twenty-two months of exposure cannot establish durability, cumulative harm or resistance in a drug that might be taken for decades. Nothing here applies to sporadic disease, where the driving lesion is not VHL loss. NCCN states that data for larger tumours, locally advanced unresectable tumours and distant disease are extremely limited and that trials are ongoing. [PAYER]
alt.note: One correction from the full-text read: the first draft of this page said the trial does not report a response rate for pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours separately. It does - 20 of 22 (91%), which ENETS quotes as 90.9%. The comparison of 327 lifetime tumour-reduction procedures before treatment against 3 afterwards is not a like-for-like rate; the authors' own figure records 64 procedures in the preceding 2.5 years, which is.

alt.t: MEN4, NF1 and tuberous sclerosis: manage on clinical judgement, and say that is what you are doing.
alt.pref: Pancreatic tumours are rare in NF1 and tuberous sclerosis, and in tuberous sclerosis they are typically small, well-differentiated and often functional, in the body or tail, with insulin-secreting tumours common; resection of a functional tumour to cure the hormone excess is indicated when safe. MEN4 is newly described, penetrance estimates and surveillance guidelines are not available, and NCCN allows following the MEN1 surveillance recommendations given the clinical overlap.
alt.avoid: Do not present any of this as evidence based. By 2012 only 10 tuberous-sclerosis-associated pancreatic NETs had been reported, and NANETS states that no evidence-based surveillance or treatment recommendation can be made.

avoid.t: Do not operate for a hormonal syndrome in MEN1 on the assumption that the biggest visible tumour is the source.
avoid.pref: Attempt preoperative localisation of the functional tumour specifically, and use intraoperative ultrasonography routinely. Refer to a high-volume endocrine surgery centre.
avoid.avoid: NANETS warns that multiplicity makes definitive preoperative determination that the dominant tumour is the source of hormone overproduction difficult, and that hypergastrinaemia in MEN1 much more often arises from duodenal gastrinomas than from pancreatic tumours. Resecting the dominant nodule and finding the syndrome unchanged is a recognised outcome. [EXPERTISE]

avoid.t: Do not use a VHL tumour's location in the head as a reason to resect it earlier.
avoid.pref: Decide on size, doubling time and mutation; let location decide only which operation is performed.
avoid.avoid: The earlier proposal of a 2 cm threshold in the head and 3 cm in the body and tail was motivated by a wish to avoid a future pancreatoduodenectomy, not by biology. NANETS states that there is no evidence of any difference in biological behaviour by anatomic location and therefore no evidence that size criteria should be influenced by it — see the flagged item below.

gates.name: 8 · High grade: G3 tumour or neuroendocrine carcinoma
crit: Ki-67 above 20% or more than 20 mitoses per 2 mm²
Well-differentiated morphology with a high proliferative index — a G3 NET
Small-cell or large-cell poorly differentiated morphology — a neuroendocrine carcinoma
A mixed neuroendocrine–non-neuroendocrine neoplasm, each component at least 30%
Grade progression in a tumour previously called G1 or G2
gates.ask: Ki-67 is 34% — is this a well-differentiated G3 tumour I can still operate on, or a carcinoma that needs platinum this week?

standard.t: A localised well-differentiated G3 tumour is evaluated for resection with regional lymphadenectomy, after multidisciplinary review, with a clinical trial preferred where one exists.
standard.pref: NCCN's locoregional G3 page offers clinical trial as the preferred option, or resection with regional lymphadenectomy if appropriate after multidisciplinary review, or neoadjuvant systemic therapy case by case where the Ki-67 is 55% or above. NANETS: patients with high-grade well-differentiated tumours should be evaluated for resection if localised, in the context of multimodal therapy.
standard.avoid: Be honest about what resection achieves here. In 310 resected patients, the 24 with G3 tumours had 5-year overall survival of 20% (relative risk 13.56 against G1) compared with 91% for G1 and 71% for G2; among the G3 patients, those without metastases reached 43% at 5 years and those with metastases 0% (35% at 2 years). In 119 high-grade tumours from 10 Nordic centres, 85% were metastatic at diagnosis; of 14 resected patients without metastases, 13 developed metastases and the fourteenth a local recurrence, at a median of 7 months.
standard.note: The 310-patient and 119-patient resected series quoted above are taken from the NANETS consensus text and are not in this page's full-text depot. The 305-patient Nordic study of advanced gastrointestinal neuroendocrine carcinoma that is in the depot concerns unresectable disease and bears on this gate only through its prognostic findings: median survival was 11 months (95% CI 9.4-12.6) with palliative chemotherapy and 1 month (0.3-1.8) with best supportive care, but the untreated group was twelve years older with 52% at performance status 3-4, so that contrast is late referral rather than a treatment effect. Pancreatic primaries, 71 of the 305, had the longest median survival of any site - 15 months against 8 for colonic, p=0.01 across sites - and were more often receptor-positive (46% against 0-25%, p=0.001). Performance status dominated the final model: median survival 18 months at PS 0, 12 at PS 1 and 5 at PS 2, alongside primary site, platelets below 400 and a normal lactate dehydrogenase. There is no role for adjuvant therapy here outside a trial.

standard.t: Do not resect a poorly differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine carcinoma for cure; treat it as a carcinoma.
standard.pref: NANETS states that patients with poorly differentiated carcinoma, small or large cell, should not undergo resection, given the aggressive behaviour and extremely poor prognosis that does not appear to be affected by surgery. ENETS 2023 allows that surgery can benefit localised disease after extensive preoperative imaging, and places carboplatin with etoposide first line in metastatic disease, with irinotecan and a fluoropyrimidine as the best-evidenced second line; median survival in metastatic disease is 11 to 12 months.
standard.avoid: Do not read the two guidelines as agreeing. NANETS is close to absolute; ENETS leaves a door open for genuinely localised disease after thorough imaging. Where they do agree is that cytoreduction of liver metastases is not indicated in this histology because of high relapse rates and poor survival, and that chemotherapy comes first.
standard.note: Immunotherapy plays a minor role in biomarker-unselected patients. Molecular profiling is encouraged to identify new targets, which is a statement about the research agenda rather than about today's treatment. The ENETS digestive neuroendocrine carcinoma guidance is cited on this page from the programme-supplied guideline text and was not part of the full-text depot read for this revision.

alt.t: Treat the Ki-67 55% split as a prompt for discussion rather than a decision rule - it is not independently prognostic in the study that produced it.
alt.pref: NCCN offers neoadjuvant systemic therapy case by case where the Ki-67 is 55% or above. The cut point comes from 305 patients with advanced gastrointestinal neuroendocrine carcinoma at twelve Nordic centres, in whom the first-line response rate to platinum was 15% below 55% against 42% at or above it (p<0.001). Platinum schedule made no difference to response or survival, small-cell and non-small-cell morphology made no difference either (median survival 12 against 11 months), and later lines retained activity - second-line response 18%, third-line 7%, platinum reintroduction after a break 15%.
alt.avoid: Do not use 55% to decide an operation. The cut point was derived by receiver-operating-characteristic analysis in 42 randomly selected patients and then applied to the rest of the same cohort with no external validation; median survival was longer below it, not above it (14 against 10 months, p<0.001, with 30-month survival 23% against 7%); and it dropped out of both the full and the final multivariable models because of its strong association with primary site, so the paper's signature marker is not independently prognostic in its own analysis - a point the abstract does not convey. Ki-67 was read by many pathologists in several countries with no central review, and response was assessed by RECIST 1.0 from radiological reports rather than from measured target lesions. The regression producing the final model ran on 170 of 252 chemotherapy patients.
alt.note: What the model did retain was performance status (PS 0 odds ratio 0.24, 0.14-0.42, p<0.001), primary tumour site (p=0.007), platelets below 400 x 10^9 (0.47, 0.31-0.72) and a normal lactate dehydrogenase (0.50, 0.32-0.78). See approval 6.

alt.t: In a mixed neuroendocrine–non-neuroendocrine neoplasm, have each component diagnosed and graded, and stage by the non-neuroendocrine counterpart.
alt.pref: NCCN requires each component to be diagnosed and graded separately where the smaller component is at least 30% of the tumour mass. Extrapulmonary carcinomas, including these mixed neoplasms, are staged according to the organ-specific criteria for their non-neuroendocrine counterpart — for the pancreas, that means adenocarcinoma staging.
alt.avoid: There is no pathway for this entity. NCCN calls management controversial and notes that chemotherapy regimens directed at the non-neuroendocrine component may be considered. Do not pretend a decision rule exists.

avoid.t: Do not route a high-grade tumour to a pathway on the Ki-67 alone.
avoid.pref: Differentiation first, then grade. NCCN says it in the plainest terms available: not all high-grade neoplasms with Ki-67 above 20% are poorly differentiated.
avoid.avoid: Treating a well-differentiated G3 tumour as a small-cell carcinoma costs a patient a potentially curative operation - median disease-specific survival in well-differentiated tumours with a morphologically apparent high-grade component was 55 months (range 16-119), with 2-year and 5-year survival 88-89% and 48-49%, against 16 months and 24% and 24% for true pancreatic poorly differentiated carcinoma. Treating a carcinoma as a NET costs weeks that patient does not have. NCCN's own statement is that advanced carcinoma patients should be considered for chemotherapy without delay.
avoid.note: Two cautions from the full-text read. First, the 55-against-16-month contrast is unmatched: once stage IV was matched, pancreatic grade 1-2 tumours and those with a high-grade component did not differ significantly in disease-specific survival, and both did far better than poorly differentiated carcinoma (median 61 against 16 months, p<0.001), which is the result most corrosive to a sharp prognostic split between the first two. The first draft of this page gave 11 months for the carcinoma comparator; the paper's figure is 16. Second, the Ki-67 55% cut point NCCN uses is not independently prognostic in its own derivation study - see the reasonable-alternative item above and approval 6.

avoid.t: Do not give adjuvant systemic therapy after resection of a high-grade tumour outside a trial.
avoid.pref: Enrol in a clinical trial. NCCN states there is no role for adjuvant therapy outside one and asks for trial enrolment to be considered.
avoid.avoid: The temptation is strong because relapse is near-universal, but nothing establishes benefit, and the only comparative data in this disease — propensity-matched NCDB — found worse survival in the adjuvant group (P=0.037).

gates.name: 9 · After resection, and where this page ends
crit: A completely resected primary tumour
An observed tumour being followed on the same schedule
Grade, nodal status and perineural invasion known from the specimen
Functional syndrome status, for biochemical follow-up
Recurrence found — local, pancreatic remnant, or hepatic
gates.ask: What am I scanning for, how often, for how long, and what do I do the day a liver lesion appears?

standard.t: There is no established adjuvant therapy after resection of a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour — say so rather than offering something.
standard.pref: Every resected patient. NCCN states flatly that there is no known role for systemic treatment in the adjuvant setting, and repeats it on the grade 1–2 and grade 3 pages. A randomised trial of chemotherapy after resection is ongoing (NCT05040360) and is the right place for a patient who wants treatment.
standard.avoid: Do not improvise. The only comparative data are a propensity-matched NCDB analysis of 301 patients receiving perioperative systemic therapy against 301 having surgery alone, in which the adjuvant group did worse (P=0.037) - a result that is almost certainly selection rather than harm, since the agents were not recorded, but which does not support treating. That analysis is quoted from the NANETS and NCCN text and is not in this page's full-text depot.
standard.note: Somatostatin analogues are not adjuvant therapy. Their antiproliferative evidence is in advanced disease, the only prospective study in small tumours is in MEN1 and was not randomised (see gate 7), and ENETS states plainly that no evidence supports somatostatin analogues for controlling the progression of a small nonfunctioning tumour under surveillance.

standard.t: Follow the schedule: imaging at 12 weeks to 12 months, then every 6 to 12 months to a maximum of 10 years, then as clinically indicated.
standard.pref: History and examination, multiphasic abdomen with or without pelvis CT or MRI, chest CT as clinically indicated, and biochemical markers for functional tumours as clinically indicated. Earlier if symptoms. Use the same modality and contrast agent each time. For high-grade disease the interval is shorter: every 12 to 24 weeks for 2 years, then every 6 to 12 months for up to 10 years depending on biology and Ki-67.
standard.avoid: Receptor-based imaging and FDG-PET are not recommended for routine surveillance. Do not stop at 5 years in a G2 or node-positive patient: recurrences appear at a median of 5.1 years after resection of small tumours in the matched case-control series, at a median of 43 months in the three-centre European cohort of G1-G2 non-functional tumours, and at a median of 7.2 years for pancreatic primaries in the Ontario population cohort behind the published follow-up recommendations, where cumulative recurrence reached 33.5% at 5 years and 48.5% at 10. Ten-year overall survival after resection is 37.7% across the whole resected National Cancer Data Base population. ENETS tells patients to expect at least 20 years of surveillance and possibly lifelong. The tail of this disease is long.
standard.note: This schedule is consensus, not trial-derived, and the three consensus sources disagree with one another. NCCN starts at 12 weeks to 12 months and runs to a maximum of 10 years. ENETS 2023 starts at 3 to 6 months with a somatostatin-receptor PET, then every 6 to 12 months for 5 years, every 12 to 24 months to 10 years and then every 5 years, at level 5 evidence graded B - an inversion the GRADE framework it claims to follow would not permit. The RAND/UCLA follow-up recommendations for completely resected gastroenteropancreatic tumours deliberately de-intensify the first three years - yearly imaging for 3 years, then every 1 to 2 years to 10, with the decision to continue or stop discussed with the patient at 10 - while extending beyond 10, and exempt a grade 1, node-negative pancreatic tumour under 2 cm from follow-up altogether. That exemption came from a 22-member panel at a 75% agreement threshold, over an evidence base of 6 eligible studies plus two then-unpublished cohorts that carried no grade, stage or margin data - the very variables the recommendations stratify on. It is not adopted here. All three agree on one thing: no serum or urine biomarker has a routine role, and an isolated rise in chromogranin A is not an indication to change treatment without radiological progression. See approval 13.

standard.t: Risk-stratify the surveillance intensity on grade, nodal status and perineural invasion rather than on size.
standard.pref: In 211 curatively resected G1 and G2 non-functional tumours at three high-volume European centres, followed a median of 51 months, 35 (17%) recurred at a median of 43 months (IQR 23-62), 91% within 5 years and 69% in the pancreatic remnant; 5- and 10-year disease-specific survival were 98% and 84% and overall survival 91% and 68%. The independent predictors of recurrence within 5 years were grade 2 (HR 4.07, 95% CI 1.87-8.84, p<0.001), lymph node metastasis (HR 2.44, 1.17-5.09, p=0.017) and perineural invasion (HR 2.38, 1.11-5.10, p=0.026), and the resulting score discriminated well internally (Harrell c-statistic 0.81, 95% CI 0.75-0.87) and calibrated adequately (Hosmer-Lemeshow chi-square 11.25, p=0.258). Of 107 patients with none of the three factors, 2 recurred.
standard.avoid: Grade D on the full-text read, and the score has not been shown to add to grading: WHO grade alone gave a c-statistic of 0.72 (0.64-0.79) and the difference between the two was p=0.059, so by the paper's own test it is not better than grade. Its cut-off of 24 was selected by receiver-operating-characteristic analysis in the same data by both Youden index and log-rank, so 91% sensitivity is optimistic by construction and 62% specificity does not discriminate clinically. External validation was still ongoing at publication and the authors chose to publish without it. All three components are postoperative findings, so the instrument cannot inform whether to operate, only how often to scan afterwards. Imaging intensity during follow-up was explicitly keyed to chromogranin A, grade and nodal status, so the score's predictors also predicted the chance of detecting a recurrence - a surveillance bias the authors note and do not adjust for. The cohort excluded MEN1, VHL, grade 3 and all metastatic disease, so the 17% recurrence rate and the 2-of-107 figure apply to a cleaner population than clinic presents. In the sub-2 cm subgroup, which is what any size threshold needs, there were 4 recurrence events in 84 patients and the univariable hazard ratios span two orders of magnitude (perineural invasion 30.7, 95% CI 3.19-295.74); no multivariable model was possible and none should be inferred. The work was funded by Ipsen and its stated purpose is to identify high-risk patients for future adjuvant therapy trials.
standard.note: In MEN1 the remnant is the problem rather than the margin: local intrapancreatic recurrence unrelated to margin status is reported as high as 50%, so a MEN1 patient's surveillance is lifelong and is about new disease, not about this operation.

standard.t: When hepatic metastases appear, this becomes the NELM pathway — hand the patient over by name and keep the pancreatic history with them.
standard.pref: The NELM page is where hepatic burden and distribution, cytoreduction thresholds, liver-directed modality selection, systemic sequencing, carcinoid-crisis precautions and the transplant question live. Two facts from this page travel with the patient and change what that page can offer: whether a pancreatoduodenectomy has been done, because liver-directed therapy afterwards carries an increased risk of cholangitis and liver abscess; and whether a cholecystectomy was performed, because long-term somatostatin analogue therapy raises the risk of biliary symptoms and cholecystitis.
standard.avoid: Do not start systemic therapy for hepatic metastases on this page. Do not restage with a pancreas-only protocol. And do not let a transplant-relevant patient be committed to a pancreatic reoperation before the NELM page's transplant gate has been asked, since Milan-NET criteria require the primary to have been resected with all extrahepatic disease and a documented disease-free interval.
standard.note: Resection of recurrent locoregional disease, an isolated distant metastasis, or a previously unresectable tumour that has regressed should be considered for selected patients with adequate performance status — that is NCCN's position and it is the one circumstance where this page and the NELM page are deciding the same operation together.

alt.t: Receptor PET has a defined place in follow-up, and it is not routine imaging.
alt.pref: The appropriate-use indications NANETS reproduces are three: monitoring disease seen predominantly on receptor PET; restaging at clinical or biochemical progression without progression on conventional imaging; and a new indeterminate lesion on conventional imaging with unclear progression. Where disease is visible on both and conventional imaging is stable, intermittent PET every 2 to 3 years may help; where the tumour is readily seen on CT or MRI, receptor PET is not needed for monitoring.
alt.avoid: The supporting evidence is thin and mostly expert opinion. NANETS reports that in 63 patients imaged after resection sensitivity and specificity for recurrence were 92% and 80%, and that in a 143-patient multicentre follow-up cohort receptor imaging detected 75.8% (132 of 174) of new lesions and 29.3% (51 of 174) that CT had missed, being judged useful in 73.4% of patients - but "useful" was defined as changing a subsequent action, not as changing an outcome, and neither series is in this page's full-text depot. The SNMMI/EANM procedure standard, which is, gives no guidance at all on whether or how to use receptor PET in a small pancreatic lesion under surveillance, and warns that an increase or decrease in lesional uptake must not be taken as an indicator of response or progression the way it would be with other radiotracers - which removes the obvious use. The standard also carries no systematic review, no evidence grading and no strength-of-recommendation scheme, so a prospective trial and a package insert carry equal weight in it.

alt.t: Manage the sequelae of the operation as part of follow-up, not as someone else's problem.
alt.pref: New endocrine and exocrine insufficiency is the commonest durable harm of this pathway and it is measurable. In a random-effects meta-analysis of 22 observational comparative studies (1,148 patients: 432 enucleations against 716 standard resections), enucleation gave less endocrine insufficiency (risk difference -0.08, 95% CI -0.12 to -0.04, p<0.001, I-squared 0%) and less exocrine insufficiency (-0.17, -0.31 to -0.04, p=0.01, I-squared 86%). NANETS adds that after central pancreatectomy endocrine and exocrine insufficiency rates were 4% and 5% against 24% and 17% after distal pancreatectomy and 17% and 29% after pancreatoduodenectomy. Screen for both, and for pancreatic exocrine deficiency in anyone on long-term analogue therapy. ENETS adds the late iatrogenic harms to screen for after systemic treatment: renal dysfunction after streptozotocin or peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, heart failure after sunitinib or doxorubicin, and marrow effects after radionuclide therapy or alkylating agents.
alt.avoid: Do not count a resection a success on imaging alone in a patient who now has diabetes they did not have, for a tumour that might have been observed. And do not read the functional advantage as an effect of the operation alone: the review concedes it cannot tell whether the standard-resection patients were ever enucleation candidates, the indications pooled are insulinoma, non-functioning tumours, serous and mucinous cystadenoma, IPMN and chronic pancreatitis, mean methodological quality was 13 of a possible 27, only one of the 22 studies reported information on principal confounders, and the exocrine result carries I-squared 86% across 5 studies with no standardised definition or timing of assessment.

avoid.t: Do not surveil an observed primary less carefully than a resected one.
avoid.pref: NCCN applies the same surveillance schedule to patients in whom observation was chosen. The whole safety case for observation rests on detecting growth, and the crossover rates in the published cohorts are the mechanism by which that case holds, or fails to: 26 of 104 (25%) over a median of 30 months in the matched case-control series, 9 of 406 (2%) over 25 months in ASPEN, and 6 of 76 (8%) over 17 months in PANDORA. Read each of them as the full text reports it. In the first, the crossovers stay in the observation arm by intention to treat, so part of that arm's clean record was bought with the operation the paper argues can be avoided. In PANDORA, six of the eight patients who met the protocol's own resection criterion refused the operation, so the protocol was never tested. And in ASPEN only 4 of 406 surveillance patients came to surgery for growth at all.
avoid.avoid: An observed tumour with no owner and no interval is not being observed. This is the single most likely way for this pathway to fail a patient.

avoid.t: Do not use routine FDG-PET or receptor PET as a surveillance scan.
avoid.pref: Multiphasic CT or MRI on the schedule above, with the functional scans reserved for the three appropriate-use situations.
avoid.avoid: NCCN states that receptor-based imaging and FDG-PET are not recommended for routine surveillance. Receptor PET also has not been shown to add significantly to conventional imaging for assessing response to peptide receptor radionuclide therapy.

quickref.foot: The evidence is three uncontrolled cohorts, none randomised and none of which compares the two strategies, plus one systematic review that does and found nothing. Sadot 2016: 104 observed matched on initial size to 77 resected, inclusion band under 3 cm rather than 2 cm with median lesion 1.2-1.4 cm and 87% T1; 26 of 104 (25%) resected later at a median of 30 months and retained in the observation arm by intention to treat; median size unchanged at 1.2 cm (p=0.7) although 53 of 104 (51%) grew; no observed patient developed metastases; median follow-up 44 months overall but only 33 months (IQR 11-72) in the patients never operated, against recurrences at a median of 5.1 years in the resected arm; the metastasis-free survival advantage of 99% against 88% (p=0.01) is an endpoint artefact and disappears in the observation-only comparison (p=0.08); 21% grade 3 complications in the resected. PANDORA: 76 patients with tumours of 2 cm or less, median follow-up 17 months; 8 (11%) growing by more than 0.5 cm per year of whom 6 refused the protocol-mandated operation; one occult nodal plus peritoneal metastasis at 2.0 cm; only 22% had the scheduled 3-month endoscopic ultrasound; baseline quality of life worse than the reference population. ASPEN interim: 500 patients at 41 centres, 406 surveillance and 94 surgery, median follow-up 25 months (IQR 16-35), 9 of 406 (2%) coming to surgery, severe complications in 13% of the resected with no deaths - and two findings that cut the other way, distant metastases in 4 of 500 (0.8%, printed in the paper as 0.08%) all present at diagnosis, and one or more aggressive histological features in 19 of 94 resected tumours (20%), a figure that comes only from the resected and cannot describe the 406 watched. The threshold does not survive a ROC analysis: in 5,172 SEER patients the cutoff best associated with a composite aggressiveness outcome was 2.50 cm (AUC 0.769, sensitivity 81.3%, specificity 63.3%), and 1-2 cm against 1 cm or less was not prognostic for survival (HR 0.92, 0.65-1.31, p=0.652). And it may not hold across populations: nodal metastasis below 2 cm was 5% and 12% in white patients against 23% and 21% in Black patients in two overlapping resected datasets (p<0.01 in both), with the sub-1 cm finding failing to replicate.
