honest.t: The 2 cm threshold is an operating convention that has hardened into a biological claim, and the full-text read makes that worse rather than better. This page uses it as the point at which the conversation changes, not as a boundary between benign and malignant.
honest.why: Grade C at best and arguably D. No study randomises observation against resection at this size, none is powered for disease-specific survival, not one of the three cohorts behind the threshold performs any comparison between the two strategies, and the longest prospective follow-up is 25 months in a disease whose recurrences arrive at a median of 4 to 7 years. The only systematic comparison that exists anywhere - 37 studies, 1,814 patients, run for the 2025 MEN1 recommendations - found no difference in metastasis or mortality between surgery and surveillance for lesions of 2 cm or less, at low to very low GRADE certainty. A receiver-operating-characteristic analysis of 5,172 SEER patients put the optimal cutoff for a composite aggressiveness outcome at 2.50 cm with 63% specificity, and in the same dataset 1-2 cm against 1 cm or less was not prognostic for survival at all. Meanwhile 4 of 500 ASPEN patients (0.8%) with tumours of 2 cm or less had distant metastases at diagnosis. The number is defensible as a trigger for a discussion and indefensible as a statement about biology.

honest.t: The paper most often cited for the 2 cm threshold never tested it.
honest.why: Sadot 2016's inclusion band was 3 cm or less, not 2 cm, and in practice median lesion size was 1.2 cm in the observed group and 1.4 cm in the resected with 87% T1 - so its evidence concerns tumours of about a centimetre and it is silent about the 2-3 cm range it nominally covers. Three further features change what it can be cited for. Twenty-six of 104 observed patients (25%) had an operation and remain in the observation arm by intention to treat, so part of that arm's clean oncological record was purchased with the surgery the paper argues can be avoided. The patients genuinely never operated were followed a median of 33 months against a median time to recurrence of 5.1 years in the resected arm, so the arm was not watched long enough to experience the event reported as absent. And the metastasis-free survival advantage for observation, 99% against 88%, p=0.01, is an artefact of the endpoint rather than a finding - a resected patient can be recorded as recurring and an unresected patient with stable imaging cannot - and it disappears in the observation-only comparison (p=0.08). Fifty-one per cent of observed tumours did grow; the unchanged median size of 1.2 cm conceals that 53 grew, 19 were static and 32 shrank. Thirty-five per cent of the observation group never had tissue at all.

honest.t: ASPEN's 20% rate of aggressive histology, which this page used as the counterweight to a flat 2 cm rule, cannot describe the patients who were watched.
honest.why: The figure is 19 of 94 - and those 94 are the resected patients, a denominator selected by radiological size over 10 mm (OR 1.9), a main pancreatic duct over 3 mm (OR 3.4), age 64 or under (OR 2.5), enrolment at a surgical centre (OR 2.0) and a HADS anxiety score of 4-6 (OR 2.0). It is the prevalence of aggressive biology among people chosen for an operation, not among sub-2 cm lesions, and certainly not among the 406 who were surveilled. The surveillance arm has no histological characterisation at all: a third of patients never had an aspirate and grade was not evaluable in a quarter of those who did. Follow-up was 25 months, crossover 2%, allocation was by the referring centre, and the paper performed no comparison between the two strategies. Its metastasis rate is printed as 0.08 per cent when 4 of 500 is 0.8 per cent, a tenfold understatement of its own safety signal that remains uncorrected. ASPEN was funded by ENETS, whose surveillance recommendation is the hypothesis under test, and senior authors wrote that recommendation. It is the best prospective evidence in this disease and it still cannot answer the question.

honest.t: PANDORA did not test the protocol it is cited for.
honest.why: Six of the eight patients who met the study's own criterion for resection - growth beyond 0.5 cm per year - refused the operation and continued watchful waiting, so the cohort's benign course reflects patient choice rather than a protocol that was followed and held. Adherence failed elsewhere too: only 17 of 76 (22%) had the scheduled 3-month endoscopic ultrasound, 19 (25%) were enrolled on a single imaging modality against a protocol requiring two, and 28% and 15% had no imaging at all at 6 and 12 months, so progression could have been missed rather than absent. Eligibility excluded patients whose lesion already looked malignant, which is exactly the population whose risk decides whether waiting is safe. Seventy-six patients at a median of 17 months cannot support a statement about oncological safety, and the single most informative event in the study cuts against it: a lesion that grew from 1.8 to 2.6 cm proved at operation to be a 2.0 cm tumour with two positive nodes and peritoneal metastasis. One resected lesion was not a neuroendocrine tumour at all.

honest.t: The nodal-risk literature that justifies operating on small tumours is entirely a resected-population literature, and that is a structural defect rather than a caveat.
honest.why: Every figure this page quotes for nodal metastasis below 2 cm comes from a cohort in which every patient was operated. Hashim's 136 patients were drawn from a surgical database at a unit that states its own institutional bias toward complete oncological resection, and the authors acknowledge that patients selected for observation were not included before drawing a management conclusion from the dataset anyway; its claim that no preoperative variable defines a low-risk group is therefore generated from a population in which the low-risk tail is structurally absent, and its headline 12% rate in tumours of 1 cm or less is 2 of 17 patients. Zheng-Pywell's racial comparison and Makris's imaging-feature analysis share the same design, and Makris's authors concede they cannot even identify which patients were managed non-operatively. The National Cancer Data Base, which supplies the 29% nodal and 10% distant rates, records only tumours assigned a malignant behaviour code and so removes precisely the indolent lesions a surveillance policy concerns. There is no cohort anywhere that reports nodal status in unoperated small tumours, because obtaining it requires the operation under debate. This page therefore cannot state a nodal risk for the patient in front of you, and should not pretend to.

honest.t: The ENETS position on the 1-2 cm band was mis-stated in the first draft of this page, and the correction matters.
honest.why: The ENETS 2023 nonfunctioning pancreatic NET guidance was available only as its abstract when this page was drafted, and the position was taken from how NANETS and the ASPEN investigators report it: observation considered for lesions no larger than 2 cm. The full text, read on 7 October 2026, says something different and narrower. ENETS recommends active surveillance for an asymptomatic tumour of 1 cm or less without main pancreatic duct dilation; it personalises the band above 1 cm up to 2 cm to the resection that would be required and the patient's comorbidities, with no decision rule offered; and it strongly recommends surgery for any nonfunctioning tumour larger than 2 cm or with main duct dilation. All three carry level 3 evidence and grade B, and the strongest wording in the document is reserved for the threshold above which it operates. So the three guidelines are closer together at 1 cm and further apart above it than this page previously said, and the 1-2 cm band is handed back to the clinician by all three.

honest.t: A dilated main pancreatic duct is treated here as a strong reason to resect a small nonfunctional tumour, and the supporting data are weaker than that posture implies.
honest.why: This follows the ASPEN authors and ENETS rather than NCCN, which does not list duct dilatation as a resection trigger anywhere in its algorithm. ASPEN's authors state that surgery is always mandatory with a dilated duct, and ENETS strongly recommends it - but the underlying observation is association, not outcome: a duct above 3 mm was independently associated with the decision to operate (OR 3.4, p<0.001), and duct dilatation was the stated indication in 11 of 94 operations. The histological evidence is thinner than it reads. Of the 19 resected tumours with an aggressive feature, 17 were radiologically over 10 mm and the remaining 2 had a dilated duct - but only 5 of the 19 had a radiological duct over 3 mm at all. So duct dilatation identified the two aggressive sub-centimetre lesions and most aggressive lesions did not have it. Grade D as a rule, and it needs ratification. See approval 2.

honest.t: Whether the size threshold should differ by race is unresolved, and the full-text read makes the evidence thinner rather than stronger.
honest.why: The signal is real and worth taking seriously: nodal metastasis below 2 cm was 7 of 30 (23%) in Black patients against 8 of 151 (5%) in white patients in the study group cohort and 54 of 258 (21%) against 188 of 1,596 (12%) in the national database, both p<0.01, with no difference in any larger band, and tumour size predicted nodal metastasis in white patients only. But the policy-relevant cell is 7 of 30, the sub-1 cm claim is 2 of 8 and it fails to replicate in the validation cohort (10% against 9%, p=0.66) - which the paper reports and then does not let alter its conclusion. The two datasets overlap institutionally, so the validation partly re-analyses the same patients. Every patient in both was resected with nodes removed. Grade was excluded from one dataset and is unavailable in the other, so the difference may track grade. Race was recorded administratively with no measure of insurance, income, referral delay or access to imaging, any of which would produce the same association, and the group's own earlier finding that node-negative Black patients had better recurrence-free survival is quoted in the discussion and left unreconciled. Six size strata across two datasets with no correction for multiple comparisons. It is strong enough to require a local position and an annual audit, and not strong enough for this page to state one. See approval 3.

honest.t: Lymphadenectomy is done here to stage the patient and to make the next decision possible, not because it has been shown to treat the disease - and the 11-to-15 node target is not this disease's number.
honest.why: Grade C for the prognostic value of nodal status and grade D for the act and for the count. The 11-to-15 figure is derived from the yield of finding a positive node rather than from any outcome, is borrowed from the pancreatic adenocarcinoma literature, and the primary study behind it is not in this page's full-text depot; NANETS itself states there is no universally accepted minimum node number for prognostication here, and ENETS draws the line at 3 cm instead. In the National Cancer Data Base analysis of tumours of 2 cm or less, adding a lymphadenectomy made no difference to 2-year or 5-year survival - though nodes examined differed systematically by operation (63% of partial pancreatectomies against 89% of pancreatoduodenectomies), so that comparison is between groups with different staging completeness and is uninformative either way. And in the 136-patient cohort read in full, nodal status predicted disease-free survival strongly (median 4.5 against 14.6 years) while overall survival did not reach significance (log-rank 0.1), and multivariable analysis identified no independent predictor of nodal metastasis at all.

honest.t: The surveillance intervals on this page are consensus throughout, the same intervals are applied to an observed tumour as to a resected one because NCCN says to, and the three consensus sources contradict each other.
honest.why: Grade D. No trial compares surveillance schedules in this disease. NCCN starts at 12 weeks to 12 months and runs to 10 years. ENETS 2023 starts at 3 to 6 months and runs past 10 to a stated expectation of at least 20 years and possibly lifelong, at level 5 evidence graded B. The RAND/UCLA follow-up recommendations - the source this page borrows its structure from - deliberately de-intensify the first three years to yearly imaging and extend past ten, and exempt a grade 1, node-negative pancreatic tumour under 2 cm from any follow-up at all. That exemption rests on a 22-member panel at a 75% agreement threshold, in a dataset whose cumulative recurrence was 33.5% at 5 years and 48.5% at 10 and whose median time to pancreatic recurrence was 7.2 years, and node-negative in a small tumour usually means few or no nodes were removed. This page does not adopt it, but it cannot claim its intervals are evidence-based when the paper it borrows from says something else. The safety case for observation rests entirely on detecting growth, and the interval that detects it has never been determined empirically. See approval 13.

honest.t: No growth threshold in use has been derived, and the two in circulation disagree by a factor of five.
honest.why: PANDORA used more than 0.5 cm per year; the 2025 MEN1 recommendations use under 1 mm per year as the point at which the interval can be lengthened, at 92% panel agreement. Neither has a cited derivation. One millimetre a year lies below the measurement reproducibility of serial cross-sectional imaging of a small pancreatic lesion across different scanners and readers, so it will manufacture both false stability and false progression. Half a centimetre a year is no better founded: the 8 PANDORA patients who met it had a mean size at last follow-up of still only 1.2 cm, and only 2 ever crossed 2.0 cm, so the threshold was detecting measurement variation as much as growth. Meanwhile growth was the stated indication for surgery in only 4 of 406 ASPEN surveillance patients, against patient and centre preference in 79 of 94 operations. The programme has to pick a threshold and a measurement convention and write both down, and then say plainly that neither is derived. See approval 12.

honest.t: Enucleation is offered as a parenchyma-sparing alternative on the strength of pooled retrospective comparisons in which the enucleable tumours were, by definition, the favourable ones.
honest.why: Grade C. All 22 studies in the meta-analysis were non-randomised and observational, mean methodological quality was 13 of a possible 27, and only one of the 22 reported information on principal confounders - so the random-effects pooling is combining uncontrolled comparisons. The review concedes it cannot tell whether the standard-resection patients were ever enucleation candidates, which makes part of every difference in blood loss, operating time and pancreatic insufficiency an artefact of lesion size and position. Indications pooled insulinoma, non-functioning tumours, serous and mucinous cystadenoma, IPMN and chronic pancreatitis, so no result is specific to a neuroendocrine tumour. The functional advantages are consistent and plausible (endocrine risk difference -0.08, exocrine -0.17, the latter with I-squared 86%); the fistula excess is real (OR 2.09, 1.41-3.11) and disappeared only in four studies doing more than 20 enucleations in total and more than 4 a year - a volume threshold the review's own authors defined and inserted into their quality checklist, which makes the least pre-specified analysis the one carried into the conclusion. And the question a surveillance pathway actually needs, whether enucleation without lymphadenectomy is oncologically adequate, is the one the review states it cannot address. Local annual volume has not been set and needs to be. See approval 5.

honest.t: Grade from a needle biopsy is treated as a floor rather than a fact, and observation decisions are made on it anyway.
honest.why: Mechanistically sound and uncomfortable, and the primary study is worse than the page previously implied. The paper's title advertises high reproducibility, which is true only of two readers scoring the same slide (r-squared 0.93 and 0.94); the clinically relevant comparison, cytological against histological grade, returned a kappa of 0.21 (p=0.09), rising only to 0.24 when at least 200 cells were counted and no better at a 5% cut-off, and 10 of 14 histological G2 tumours (71%) were called cytological G1 with histological Ki-67 averaging 1.3 times the cytological value. NANETS reports agreement under 50% for G2 and G3 and areas with Ki-67 of 2% or less common within G2 tumours; the only prospective core-biopsy study enrolled 30 patients and is not in this depot. The survival separation that makes cytological grade look useful is carried by 4 cytological G3 patients, all of whom were locally advanced, node-positive or metastatic at diagnosis, and the concordance analysis could only include resected tumours - so nothing in it describes the small lesions actually being watched. We are observing some tumours whose true grade is higher than the number in the chart, and no study quantifies how often or with what consequence.

honest.t: Whether to obtain tissue at all before choosing surveillance is a live guideline disagreement that this page does not settle.
honest.why: NANETS says biopsy is not routinely necessary to confirm the diagnosis before deciding to observe an asymptomatic sub-centimetre lesion with a characteristic imaging phenotype. ENETS 2023, read in full, says a suspected nonfunctioning tumour under 2 cm with positive somatostatin-receptor imaging should be confirmed histologically or cytologically where possible (level 3, grade B), and separately flags DAXX and ATRX loss and alternative lengthening of telomeres as independent adverse prognostic factors particularly in tumours of 2 cm or less - which is an argument for tissue. The 2025 MEN1 recommendations find no role for routine EUS-guided biopsy in that syndrome. Three positions, no outcome data separating them, and a real cost either way: a biopsy that under-grades by 71% in G2 disease versus a surveillance programme with no histology at all, which is what two thirds of ASPEN's surveillance arm actually had. See approval 11.

honest.t: What to do with a receptor-positive, FDG-positive localised primary in a patient whose biopsy says G1 or G2 is not covered by any guideline, and is currently decided case by case.
honest.why: The combined-PET score is now better supported and still inapplicable here. In the 319-patient three-centre cohort it independently predicted overall survival (HR 2.376, 1.682-3.357, p<0.001) and time to progression, with inter-rater kappa 0.8 - but histological grade was independently prognostic alongside it (HR 1.615, 1.192-2.187, p=0.002), so the claim in the first draft that the score outperformed pathological grading holds only in the 62-patient derivation cohort where grade was non-significant and no multivariable model was fitted. Both cohorts were metastatic or unresectable disease; only 39% and 36% of patients had pancreatic primaries and neither paper reports a pancreatic subgroup; two of the three validation centres supplied the derivation data; and treatment was not modelled, which matters because receptor-positive, FDG-negative disease is the eligibility criterion for radionuclide therapy. The 5-point scale has never been validated level by level and carries no treatment threshold. The SNMMI/EANM standard says FDG positivity predicts progression more strongly than grade and that the combination can direct a biopsy to the worst lesion, and stops there. Applying any of it to a 1.5 cm primary is an extrapolation with no outcome data behind it either way.

honest.t: Non-localised sporadic gastrinoma is left unsettled on this page, with the two guideline positions stated side by side.
honest.why: NCCN offers observation or exploration with duodenotomy, intraoperative ultrasound and periduodenal node dissection; NANETS 2020 recommends against routine exploration and asks for referral to a centre with expertise. Norton's comparison remains the strongest datum and the full-text read sharpens what is wrong with it: 160 operated against 35 who met the same criteria but did not have surgery - 19 because they refused after consulting their own physician, 10 because MEN1 with no lesion above 2.5 cm, 5 for comorbidity - with liver metastases 5% against 29% (p=0.0002) and 15-year disease-related survival 98% against 74%. The surgical arm's disease-related figure rests on 2 deaths with no confidence interval for the ratio; non-disease mortality was numerically higher in the controls (31% against 20%), the expected signature of a sicker comparison group, reported as non-significant and not interpreted; cause of death was adjudicated unblinded by the operating investigators in a study whose endpoint is cause-specific; the controls were imaged every 6 to 12 months against yearly evaluation of the operated patients, so ascertainment differed by arm; and accrual spans 1980 to the mid-2000s during which the operation itself changed, with all 10 patients in whom no tumour was found operated before routine duodenotomy. Almost every primary was duodenal or nodal. NANETS' counter-argument - that the supporting surgical data predate modern imaging and that the tumours found at exploration were the prognostically best ones - is unrefuted. This needs a named local position and a named referral centre, not a case-by-case improvisation. See approval 4.

honest.t: The hereditary-syndrome thresholds on this page are tautologies of their own derivation, and both were downgraded on the full-text read.
honest.why: Grade D for both. The MEN1 20 mm line rests on a metastasis gradient whose two lowest strata are 1 of 25 and 4 of 40 patients with entirely overlapping confidence intervals, metastasis defined on imaging in 60% of cases in a paper that itself cites evidence that a quarter of radiographically node-negative MEN1 patients have occult metastases at operation, and a mean follow-up of 4.3 years in a disease whose victims died at a mean age of 43; the same paper's comparison of 32 curatively operated against 66 unoperated patients found no difference in metastasis, tumour death or progression, which is an underpowered null rather than equivalence. The VHL rule was derived from 9 metastatic events and then declared to capture all 9, so its perfect sensitivity is a property of the derivation; doubling time was computable in all 9 of those patients but only 54 of 99 without metastases, and patients with growing lesions are imaged more often, so the exposure and the ability to measure it are entangled; 69 of the 108 lesions were never resected and rest on imaging appearance alone, which the senior author conceded could include microcystic adenomas; the 3 cm cut point was carried over from the group's own prior work and a discussant's question about 1 and 2 cm was answered by saying the analysis had not been done; and no Ki-67 or grade datum exists anywhere in the series. Both thresholds are probably right in direction. Neither was derived.

honest.t: Calcification is reported on this page as a reason to think again about a small lesion, and its statistical support is almost absent.
honest.why: Grade D. The independent hazard ratio is 11.5 with a 95% confidence interval from 1.1 to 125.0 at p=0.043, in a Cox model that also returns 25.2 and 33.0 for nodal and distant metastasis, with no event count reported anywhere - the signature of an overfitted model. Cystic morphology, presented alongside it in the abstract and conclusion as usable for stratification, was not independently prognostic at all (HR 1.6, 0.2-14.3, p=0.69). Between 28% and 29% of the cohort has no data on the two exposures and the analysis is complete-case with no imputation or sensitivity analysis; the exposures were classified from radiology report wording across eight institutions and seventeen years with no central re-read, which makes them a measure of reporting practice as much as of biology; the cystic-and-calcified cell anchoring the four-way comparison holds 16 patients; and the paper's own Table 1 is internally inconsistent, so the denominators behind its percentages cannot be reconstructed. Median follow-up was 35 months against recurrences at 4 to 7 years. The association with adverse pathology is plausible and the direction is probably right. The effect size is uninterpretable.

honest.t: The Ki-67 55% split that NCCN uses to offer neoadjuvant therapy is not independently prognostic in the study that produced it.
honest.why: The cut point was derived by receiver-operating-characteristic analysis in 42 randomly selected patients within a 305-patient retrospective cohort of advanced gastrointestinal neuroendocrine carcinoma and then applied to the rest of that same cohort, with no external validation. It does separate platinum response (15% below 55% against 42% at or above, p<0.001) - but median survival was longer in the lower group, not the higher (14 against 10 months, p<0.001), and Ki-67 dropped out of both the full and the final multivariable models because of its strong association with primary site, a fact the abstract does not convey. Performance status, primary site, platelets and lactate dehydrogenase are what the model retained. Ki-67 was read by many pathologists in several countries with no central review and the authors say the cut-off should be interpreted with caution. Pancreatic primaries were 71 of the 305, analysed as one of seven site subgroups with no multiplicity correction. NCCN itself flags the data as limited and Ki-67 as heterogeneous within a tumour and across serial biopsies. See approval 6.

honest.t: The sharp prognostic split between a well-differentiated G3 tumour and a poorly differentiated carcinoma softens when stage is matched, and one number on the first draft of this page was wrong.
honest.why: The comparator for poorly differentiated pancreatic carcinoma is 16 months, not the 11 months this page previously carried; the first draft took the figure from the abstract rather than the table. More importantly, in the stage-matched analysis restricted to stage IV, pancreatic grade 1-2 well-differentiated tumours and those with a morphologically apparent high-grade component showed no statistically significant difference in disease-specific survival, and both did far better than carcinoma (median 61 against 16 months, p<0.001, hazard ratios 0.17 and 0.16) - which is the result most corrosive to the paper's own framing, and the abstract leads with the unmatched 55-against-162-month contrast instead. The clinical conclusion stands: differentiation, not Ki-67, decides whether an operation is on the table. But the 31 cases were found by searching two pathology archives for grade discrepancy, so nothing in the series estimates how often transformation happens; the genotype contrast that separates these tumours from carcinoma rests on 4 prospectively sequenced tumours against literature controls; and 6 of the 31 were biopsies in which the defining lower-grade component was inferred from clinical history rather than seen.

honest.t: There is no adjuvant therapy here, and the page says nothing rather than offering something.
honest.why: This is the correct reading of the evidence and it is still hard to deliver to a node-positive G2 patient with perineural invasion whose recurrence risk is substantial. The only comparative data - propensity-matched NCDB, 301 against 301 - showed worse survival with adjuvant therapy (P=0.037) with the agents unrecorded, which is almost certainly selection rather than harm but is not a reason to treat; that analysis is quoted from the NANETS and NCCN text and is not in this page's full-text depot. The randomised trial (NCT05040360) is the right answer for the patient who wants treatment. Note also what the recurrence score can and cannot do: it is internally validated only, it is not statistically better than WHO grade alone (c-statistic 0.81 against 0.72, p=0.059), all three of its components are postoperative findings, and it was funded by a somatostatin analogue manufacturer with the explicit purpose of identifying high-risk patients for adjuvant trials.

honest.t: Several numbers on this page are quoted from guideline text rather than from a primary paper read in full, and they are now labelled as such wherever they appear.
honest.why: The full-text depot read on 7 October 2026 covers 28 of the 33 indexed papers. The NANETS 2020 surgical consensus, the ENETS 2023 functioning-syndromes guidance and the ENETS 2023 digestive neuroendocrine carcinoma guidance remain the programme-supplied guideline sources rather than depot papers, and the AACE MEN1 consensus statement of March 2025 and the 2021 international consensus statement on the pancreas in MEN1 are still cited from their abstracts only - neither full text was obtained in this pass, and every numeric criterion attributed to either must be confirmed before use. Within the NANETS text specifically, the following figures carry no primary paper in this depot and should be verified against their sources before ratification: the 11-to-15 node yield; the 1,020-patient 8-centre margin series; the 310-patient and 119-patient resected high-grade series; the 326-patient nodal-survival cohort; the 999-patient and 981-patient lymphadenectomy analyses; the 63-patient and 143-patient receptor-PET follow-up series; the 44-of-107 pathology re-review; the 30-patient prospective core-biopsy study; the MD Anderson neoadjuvant series; the propensity-matched NCDB perioperative-therapy analysis; and the central-pancreatectomy insufficiency rates. Each is attributed in the body of the page where it is used.

honest.t: The NCCN version behind this page could not be established from the extracted text, and page numbers are therefore not cited anywhere.
honest.why: The programme-supplied extraction carries no version string. Its most recent references date from 2025, including the MEN1 guideline of June 2025, which places it at v3.2025 or later. Every numeric criterion attributed to NCCN on this page should be confirmed against the current published PDF before the page is used clinically, and an owner should be named for that check. See approval 10.

honest.t: The harm side of the observation-versus-resection ledger is better measured than the benefit side, and the page should be read that way.
honest.why: What the literature establishes with reasonable confidence is what an operation costs. Any grade 3 complication in 16 of 77 (21%) and a grade 3 leak-related complication in 13 (17%) in the matched case-control series; severe complications in 13% of ASPEN's resected patients with no deaths; major complications in 58 of 211 (27%) and grade B or C fistula in 46 (22%) in the three-centre recurrence cohort; a pancreatic fistula rate roughly doubled by enucleation; endocrine and exocrine insufficiency measurably reduced by parenchyma-sparing surgery and substantial after any formal resection; pancreatic resection morbidity up to 50% and mortality up to 3% even in high-volume centres on the ENETS figures. What the literature does not establish is any survival benefit from resecting a small tumour: no randomised comparison, no systematic difference in metastasis or mortality where it has been looked for, no independent effect of size, nodal status or margins on survival in the largest resected series, and no difference by extent of resection or by the addition of lymphadenectomy. A page that lists the harms precisely and the benefits vaguely is not biased - it is reporting the asymmetry in the evidence, and the conversation with the patient should carry the same asymmetry.

honest.t: There is no ratified Memorial Hermann roadmap behind this page, and the second pass has not changed that.
honest.why: Every position here was assembled from published guidelines and primary literature. The full-text read has made the page more accurate about how well supported each position is; it has not conferred any institutional authority on it. Nothing on this page has been through multidisciplinary or institutional governance review, and the fifteen approvals below are the list of decisions the group has to take before it could be.

board: Submission — a form capturing the clinical question, differentiation and the exact Ki-67, functional syndrome status with the confirmatory biochemistry, tumour size and location, main pancreatic duct calibre, calcification and cystic morphology, receptor and FDG status, nodal and hepatic status, hereditary-syndrome status or pending genetics, prior pancreatic surgery, referring clinician and urgency. Owner: submitting clinician.

Triage — a coordinator and a clinically trained gatekeeper check whether the pathology report carries a number for Ki-67 rather than a range, whether differentiation is stated, whether the imaging is a pancreas-protocol study, and whether the question is actually a decision question. A case whose Ki-67 is reported as a range goes back to pathology before it reaches the agenda. Owners: coordinator and chair.

Agenda — stable at least 24 hours ahead, with observation decisions and reassessment-interval decisions given agenda time in their own right rather than being settled in corridors. Owner: coordinator.

Urgent lane — a same-week slot with chair approval. In this disease the urgent lane is for two things: a poorly differentiated carcinoma, where NCCN asks for chemotherapy without delay, and an uncontrolled functional syndrome. A 1.2 cm nonfunctional tumour is never urgent. Owner: chair.

Attendance — hepatopancreatobiliary surgery, medical oncology, endocrinology, diagnostic radiology, nuclear medicine, advanced endoscopy, pathology, clinical genetics and coordination. Nuclear medicine and pathology are required rather than optional on this pathway, because grade and receptor status are what the gates turn on. Owners: specialty leads.

Pathology — pre-alerted for every case where differentiation is uncertain, every case where the Ki-67 will decide observation versus resection, and every high-grade neoplasm needing the Rb, p53, p16, ATRX and DAXX panel. Owner: pathology.

Genetics — a standing referral rule rather than a case-by-case judgement: every gastrinoma, every multifocal tumour, every patient under 40, and every tumour in a patient with any other MEN1-associated lesion. The genetic result is expected before an elective operation is booked. Owner: clinical genetics.

Output — one recommendation, one owner, one due date, one reassessment date, one documented alternative considered. For an observation decision the output must additionally name the imaging modality, the contrast agent, the interval and the specific finding that would trigger resection. Owner: chair.

Documentation — a note within one business day in the agreed structured format, including the exact Ki-67 and the measured tumour size in the body of the note so that the next scan can be compared with something. Owner: named owner.
Registry — the case closed with the decision, the operation performed, the resection pathology against the preoperative grade, and the outcome at reassessment. Owner: coordinator.

Referring relationships — the referring clinician is told the recommendation, the surveillance interval and who owns the next scan. Observed patients are returned to their referring clinician with a written schedule rather than retained. Owner: named owner.
dashboard: Proportion of pathology reports carrying an exact Ki-67 and an explicit differentiation statement, against those reporting a range or neither.
Preoperative grade against resection-specimen grade, for every resected patient — the local measure of how far a biopsy grade can be trusted.
Observed tumours: size, grade, duct calibre, calcification, race, and growth rate at each interval; crossover to surgery with the stated reason; and the resection pathology where crossover occurs.
Surveillance adherence for observed primaries: proportion of scans within the agreed window, and proportion using the same modality and contrast agent as the index study.
Nodes retrieved at every formal pancreatoduodenectomy and distal pancreatectomy, against the 11–15 target, and nodal positivity by tumour size band.
Enucleations per surgeon per year and in total, with pancreatic fistula grade — the volume figure the pooled fistula data depend on.
New endocrine and new exocrine insufficiency at 12 months by operation type, reported alongside the oncologic outcome rather than separately.
Severe complications (Clavien-Dindo above grade III) and 90-day mortality for resections performed on tumours of 2 cm or less, as the harm side of the observation-versus-resection ledger.
Functional tumours: localisation route, modality that found the lesion, operation, and biochemical cure at 6 months and 5 years.
Genetic referral completion for every patient meeting the standing rule, and time from diagnosis to genetic result for patients coming to elective surgery.
Hepatic recurrence: time from resection, and whether the handoff to the NELM pathway was documented with the pancreatoduodenectomy and cholecystectomy status recorded.
Observed lesions: whether tissue was obtained and by what route, against the standing rule agreed under approval 11, with cytological grade compared against resection grade in every crossover.

Measurement discipline for observed lesions: proportion of serial measurements made on the same modality, phase and contrast agent as the index study, and the proportion from which a growth rate can be recomputed from the note alone.

The harm side of the ledger, reported next to the oncologic outcome rather than separately: Clavien-Dindo above grade III, grade B or C pancreatic fistula, new endocrine and new exocrine insufficiency at 12 months, and 90-day mortality, for every resection of a tumour of 2 cm or less.
Observation decisions with the written patient statement filed, as agreed under approval 14, against the stated indication for every crossover to surgery.

approvals.q: For an incidental nonfunctional tumour of 1 to 2 cm, does the programme default to observation or to individualised decision?
approvals.why: NCCN's surgical principles say a G1 tumour under 2 cm can be safely observed and that this is the recommended course; NANETS says individualise everything between 1 and 2 cm; the Delphi consensus NANETS cites reached no agreement in that band at all; ENETS 2023, read in full, observes 1 cm or less and personalises above 1 cm to the resection required and the patient's comorbidities, with no rule offered; and the ASPEN investigators, whose data NCCN cites in support of observation, conclude that management should be personalised above 1 cm. Every source hands the 1-2 cm band back to the clinician, which means the decision is made by whoever is in the room unless a default is chosen. The full-text read adds one thing: the only systematic comparison of the two strategies at this size found no difference in metastasis or mortality, at low to very low certainty, so a default either way is a judgement and not a finding.
approvals.audit: Registry: size, grade, duct calibre, calcification, management chosen, growth, crossover to surgery with reason, resection pathology.

approvals.q: Is a dilated main pancreatic duct an absolute indication to resect a small nonfunctional tumour?
approvals.why: ASPEN's authors state that surgery is always mandatory with a dilated main pancreatic duct and ENETS 2023 strongly recommends it; NCCN does not list duct dilatation as a resection trigger anywhere. The supporting evidence is association rather than outcome - a duct above 3 mm independently predicted the decision to operate (OR 3.4, p<0.001) - and the threshold used is the study's own. The full-text read sharpens the histological argument in both directions: duct dilatation identified the only two aggressive sub-centimetre tumours in ASPEN, and yet only 5 of the 19 tumours with an aggressive feature had a radiological duct over 3 mm at all.
approvals.audit: Audit: duct calibre at diagnosis against resection pathology and against growth under observation.

approvals.q: Does the size threshold for resection differ by race?
approvals.why: Nodal metastasis below 2 cm was 23% and 21% in Black patients against 5% and 12% in white patients in two independent datasets (p<0.01 in both). NCCN reproduces the finding without altering the algorithm. The programme needs a stated position, and a stated reason for it, rather than silence.
approvals.audit: Audit: nodal positivity by size band and by race in the programme's own resected patients, reported annually.

approvals.q: What is the non-localised sporadic gastrinoma pathway, and where is it done?
approvals.why: NCCN offers observation or exploration with duodenotomy; NANETS 2020 recommends against routine exploration and asks for referral to a centre with expertise. Both cannot be the local position, and a patient who arrives with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and no target on imaging needs the answer to already exist.
approvals.audit: Registry: localisation route, operation or observation, biochemical cure at 6 months and 5 years, referral destination where used.

approvals.q: Minimum annual volume for enucleation and for central pancreatectomy at this centre.
approvals.why: The fistula excess after enucleation disappeared in pooled studies only in centres performing more than 20 in total and more than 4 a year. Central pancreatectomy carries a 35% pooled fistula rate and single-centre morbidity of 58% to 72%. These are volume-conditional operations and the threshold is a governance choice. [EXPERTISE]
approvals.audit: Audit: enucleations and central pancreatectomies per surgeon per year, fistula grade, new endocrine and exocrine insufficiency.

approvals.q: Does the group accept NCCN's 55% Ki-67 split for well-differentiated grade 3 tumours?
approvals.why: The cutoff was derived by receiver-operating-characteristic analysis in 42 randomly selected patients within a 305-patient retrospective cohort of advanced gastrointestinal neuroendocrine carcinoma and then applied to the rest of that same cohort with no external validation. Read in full, the study shows that median survival was longer below the cutoff than above it (14 against 10 months, p<0.001) and that Ki-67 dropped out of both the full and the final multivariable models because of its association with primary site - so the marker is not independently prognostic in its own derivation study. NCCN itself flags the data as limited and Ki-67 as heterogeneous within a tumour and across serial biopsies, and the one surgical series to test the line found no survival difference either side of it.
approvals.audit: Registry: Ki-67 at each biopsy, receptor and FDG status, differentiation call, treatment given, survival.

approvals.q: Who owns an observed tumour's next scan, and what happens when it is missed?
approvals.why: Not an evidence question. The entire safety case for observation rests on detecting growth, and in ASPEN patient preference and centre preference together accounted for 84% of the stated indications for surgery, with anxiety independently associated with operating. Unowned surveillance converts into an unplanned operation.
approvals.audit: Audit: surveillance adherence for observed primaries, and the stated indication for every crossover to surgery.

approvals.q: What is the standing genetic referral rule, and must the result be back before elective surgery?
approvals.why: Germline variants are reported in 16% to 21% of unselected patients, and in MEN1 or VHL the threshold, the extent and the timing of the operation all change. NCCN's criteria are a list; the programme needs a trigger that fires automatically and a rule about waiting.
approvals.audit: Audit: referral completion against the rule, time from diagnosis to result, and operations performed before the result was available.

approvals.q: How is the handoff to the NELM pathway documented, and who makes the joint decision about the primary?
approvals.why: NANETS reached no consensus on resecting a pancreatic primary when liver metastases are present. Two irreversible facts from this page constrain the NELM page — whether a pancreatoduodenectomy has been done, because liver-directed therapy afterwards carries increased cholangitis and abscess risk, and whether the gallbladder is out — so the two pathways have to decide together rather than in sequence.
approvals.audit: Registry: hepatic recurrence with pancreatoduodenectomy and cholecystectomy status recorded; documented joint decision for every primary-resection decision made in metastatic disease.

approvals.q: Who owns the NCCN, ENETS and NANETS version checks, and on what cycle?
approvals.why: The NCCN version behind this draft could not be established from the extracted text, and the MEN1 recommendations were revised twice in 2025. The ENETS nonfunctioning paper has now been read in full and its position on the 1-2 cm band corrected on this page, but the AACE MEN1 consensus statement and the 2021 international consensus statement on the pancreas in MEN1 remain abstract-only citations, and a list of figures quoted from the NANETS text with no primary paper in this page's depot is recorded in the honest section. Source reconciliation is incomplete and the page says so.
approvals.audit: Named owner plus edition and date for each guideline, with an agreed update cycle; full texts obtained for the AACE MEN1 statement and the 2021 MEN1 pancreas consensus; and each NANETS-quoted figure traced to its primary source before ratification.

approvals.q: Do we obtain tissue before choosing surveillance for a sub-2 cm nonfunctional lesion, or not?
approvals.why: NANETS says biopsy is not routinely necessary before deciding to observe a sub-centimetre lesion with a characteristic imaging phenotype. ENETS 2023, read in full, says a suspected nonfunctioning tumour under 2 cm with positive receptor imaging should be confirmed histologically or cytologically where possible (level 3, grade B). The 2025 MEN1 recommendations find no role for routine EUS-guided biopsy in that syndrome. There is no outcome evidence separating the three, and both options carry a real cost: EUS-FNA cytology called 71% of histological G2 tumours G1, while two thirds of ASPEN's surveillance arm had no evaluable histology at all. The programme needs one answer, and a stated reason.
approvals.audit: Registry: for every observed lesion, whether tissue was obtained, by what route, the cytological grade where available, and the resection grade in every patient who later crossed over.

approvals.q: What growth threshold triggers resection under surveillance, measured how, by whom, on what protocol?
approvals.why: PANDORA used more than 0.5 cm per year and the 2025 MEN1 recommendations use under 1 mm per year, a fivefold disagreement in which neither number has a cited derivation and 1 mm a year sits below the measurement reproducibility of serial imaging of a small pancreatic lesion. Growth was the stated indication for surgery in only 4 of 406 ASPEN surveillance patients, against patient and centre preference in 79 of 94 operations - so in practice the growth threshold is not what drives the operation. A threshold with a fixed modality, contrast agent, phase and measurement convention is the only version of this that can be audited.
approvals.audit: Audit: for every observed lesion, the measurement at each interval in millimetres with modality, phase and reader recorded, the computed rate, and the stated indication for every crossover.

approvals.q: Which post-resection follow-up schedule does the programme adopt, and is any patient discharged from follow-up?
approvals.why: The three consensus sources disagree. NCCN starts at 12 weeks to 12 months and runs to 10 years; ENETS 2023 starts at 3 to 6 months with a receptor PET and tells patients to expect at least 20 years and possibly lifelong; the RAND/UCLA recommendations de-intensify the first three years to yearly imaging, extend past ten and exempt a grade 1, node-negative pancreatic tumour under 2 cm from follow-up altogether - an exemption produced at a 75% agreement threshold over a dataset with no grade, stage or margin data and a 48.5% cumulative recurrence rate at 10 years. This page borrows NCCN's intervals and applies them to observed patients too. The group should choose deliberately rather than by inheritance, and decide explicitly whether anyone is discharged.
approvals.audit: Registry: schedule assigned at discharge from surgical care, adherence against it, time from resection to recurrence, and the grade and nodal status of every patient who recurred after being assigned the least intensive schedule.

approvals.q: What exactly is a patient told about the evidence for observation, and who writes it down?
approvals.why: Not an evidence question, but the read makes it a governance one. The honest statement is that no study randomises the two strategies, that the only systematic comparison found no difference at low certainty, that the harms of resection are well measured and its benefit at this size is not, that half of observed tumours grow without that meaning anything yet, and that the one thing within the programme's control is the reliability of the next measurement. A patient who is told only that small tumours can be watched safely has not been given that, and anxiety independently predicted operating in ASPEN. A written statement, the same for every patient, is cheaper than the alternative.
approvals.audit: Audit: proportion of observation decisions with the written patient statement filed, and the stated indication for every crossover to surgery recorded against it.

approvals.q: Does the programme obtain a paired receptor and FDG-PET in a localised G2 or higher primary, and what does a discordant result change?
approvals.why: FDG positivity is not rare in G1 and G2 disease and predicts progression and prognosis more strongly than grade on the SNMMI/EANM standard's own reading, and the combined score independently predicted survival in a 319-patient cohort. But both score cohorts were metastatic or unresectable, only about a third of patients had pancreatic primaries, treatment was not modelled, and the score carries no treatment threshold. If the pair is obtained and nothing is done differently, it is a cost; if something is done differently, the programme is acting beyond any published evidence and should say so and record it.
approvals.audit: Registry: receptor and FDG status at diagnosis for every localised tumour of G2 or higher, the decision taken, and the resection pathology against both.

nccn: National Comprehensive Cancer Network. Neuroendocrine and Adrenal Tumors. NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology. Version not stated in the programme-supplied extraction: its most recent references, including the MEN1 guideline of June 2025, place it at v3.2025 or later. Sections used: clinical presentations and diagnosis; nonfunctioning pancreatic tumours (evaluation, management of primary non-metastatic disease, surveillance); gastrinoma, insulinoma, glucagonoma and VIPoma pages; principles of imaging for neuroendocrine neoplasms; principles of pathology for the diagnosis of neuroendocrine neoplasms, including the 2019 WHO grading table; principles of surgical management of neuroendocrine tumours; principles of systemic anti-tumour therapy for pancreatic NET; well-differentiated grade 3 (WDG3) and poorly differentiated carcinoma (PDNEC) pages; principles of hereditary cancer risk assessment and genetic counselling; MEN1 screening, MEN1-1 and MEN1-A. The extraction is machine-converted and the layout of several algorithm pages is mangled; page numbers are deliberately not cited, and every numeric criterion must be confirmed against the current published PDF before use.
who2019: Klimstra DS, Klöppel G, La Rosa S, et al. Classification of neuroendocrine neoplasms of the digestive system. In: WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board. Digestive system tumours. 5th ed, vol 1. Lyon: International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2019. The grading criteria on this page are taken from the table NCCN reproduces from this source with permission; confirm against the current WHO volume.
nct05040360: Randomised trial of chemotherapy after resection of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, cited by NCCN as the ongoing study exploring the utility of adjuvant treatment. Named here because it is the correct destination for a resected patient who wants adjuvant therapy; the local site status and eligibility must be confirmed before a patient is counselled about it.
nelm: Memorial Hermann Neuroendocrine Liver Metastases System Roadmap, as rendered on the NELM pathway page, Draft v0.6. The destination for every patient on this page who develops or presents with hepatic metastases. It carries differentiation and grade, hepatic burden and distribution, treat-or-observe at low burden, systemic sequencing including the pancreatic-primary agents, hepatic cytoreduction, liver-directed modality selection, functional syndrome and carcinoid-crisis precautions, and the transplant gate — including the decision about resecting a pancreatic primary when liver metastases are present, where it records that NANETS 2020 reached no consensus.
firstdraft: This page is a first draft

There is no Memorial Hermann system roadmap for primary pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour and no guideline alignment worksheet for it. Every position on this page was assembled from published guidelines and primary literature for this draft; none of it has been through multidisciplinary or institutional governance review, and nothing on it should be read as an institutional decision that has been taken.
fulltext: Twenty-eight of the 33 indexed papers on this page were obtained in full text, abstracted to a fixed schema capturing setting, inclusion, exclusion, results, the authors' own stated limitations, an independent critique and a bottom line, and every evidence string on the page was checked against that abstraction. Not in the depot: the NANETS 2020 surgical consensus, the ENETS 2023 functioning-syndromes guidance and the ENETS 2023 digestive neuroendocrine carcinoma guidance, which remain the programme-supplied guideline sources; and the AACE MEN1 consensus statement of March 2025 and the 2021 international consensus statement on the pancreas in MEN1, which are still cited from their abstracts only. Figures quoted from the NANETS text with no primary paper in the depot are listed in the honest section and labelled where they are used.

provenance: Revised on 7 October 2026 after a full-text read of this page's reference depot. Twenty-eight of the 33 indexed papers were read in full and abstracted to a fixed schema recording setting, inclusion and exclusion criteria, results, the authors' own stated limitations, an independent critique and a bottom line, and every evidence string, number and grade on the page was checked against that abstraction. Thirty-nine evidence strings were changed and thirteen grades were downgraded; the gate structure, ids, names and tone values are unchanged, five previously empty recommendation slots were filled from depot papers that the first draft indexed but did not cite, the honest section grew from 12 items to 25 and the approvals list from 10 to 15. Originally built from the programme-supplied extraction of NCCN Neuroendocrine and Adrenal Tumors (version not stated in the extracted text; its most recent references, including the MEN1 guideline of June 2025, place it at v3.2025 or later) as the spine, with the NANETS 2020 consensus paper on the surgical management of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (Pancreas 2020;49:1-33) as the main surgical source, and the ENETS 2023 guidance papers for nonfunctioning pancreatic NET (J Neuroendocrinol 2023;35:e13343), for functioning pancreatic NET syndromes (e13318) and for digestive neuroendocrine carcinoma (e13249). Grading follows the WHO 2019 criteria as reproduced in the NCCN pathology principles. Liver metastases are out of scope throughout and hand off by name to the NELM pathway, which carries the hepatic decisions and the primary-resection question in metastatic disease. What the full-text read changed most is the observation-versus-resection gate. The ENETS position on the 1-2 cm band, previously taken from the abstract and from how NANETS and the ASPEN investigators report it, was wrong: the full text observes 1 cm or less, personalises 1-2 cm and strongly recommends surgery above 2 cm or with duct dilation, and the page and quick-reference table are corrected. Sadot 2016's inclusion band was 3 cm or less rather than 2 cm, so the paper most often cited for the 2 cm threshold never tested it; a quarter of its observation arm crossed to surgery and remain in it by intention to treat; the patients never operated were followed a median of 33 months against a median time to recurrence of 5.1 years in the resected arm; its metastasis-free survival advantage for observation is an endpoint artefact; and 51% of observed tumours grew. ASPEN's 20% rate of aggressive histology comes only from its 94 resected patients, a denominator selected for size, duct dilatation, age, anxiety and surgeon preference, and no comparison between strategies was performed; its metastasis rate is printed as 0.08% when 4 of 500 is 0.8%. In PANDORA, six of the eight progressing patients refused the protocol-mandated operation, so the protocol was not tested. Gratian 2014 is a National Cancer Data Base analysis rather than SEER, and the registry excludes tumours coded benign, which removes exactly the indolent lesions a surveillance policy concerns; its 33% nodal figure for sub-5 mm tumours rests on a 94-patient band in a variable missing in 45% of the cohort. The 2025 MEN1 best-practice recommendations contribute the only systematic comparison that exists: across 37 studies and 1,814 patients, surgery and surveillance for lesions under 2 cm showed no difference in metastasis or mortality at low to very low GRADE certainty. And Hashim 2014, Zheng-Pywell 2022 and Makris 2023 all draw observation-versus-resection conclusions from cohorts in which every patient was resected, which is recorded on the page as a structural defect of the nodal-risk literature rather than as a caveat. Still cited from abstract only, because no new papers were obtained in this pass: the AACE consensus statement on MEN1 of March 2025 (PMID 40232217) and the 2021 international consensus statement on the pancreas in MEN1 (PMID 32971521). Both are labelled as abstract-only wherever they are cited, and their numeric criteria must be confirmed before use. The NANETS 2020 surgical consensus and the ENETS functioning-syndromes and neuroendocrine carcinoma guidance papers were not part of the full-text depot and remain the programme-supplied guideline sources; a list of figures quoted from the NANETS text with no primary paper in the depot is recorded in the honest section and each is labelled where it is used. There is still no ratified Memorial Hermann roadmap behind this page and no alignment worksheet. It remains a draft, assembled from guidelines and primary literature, pending multidisciplinary and institutional governance review. It is not active clinical policy, it does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion on it must be verified against the current source before use.
